features.location_description: Khoraj Dabhi, Kalol taluka; XLON 72.52 YLAT 23.38
features.name: Khoraj Dabhi EWI-II

narrative.headline: A stacked deep test at Khoraj Dabhi built to separate deep confined zones
narrative.summary: Khoraj Dabhi EWI-II is one half of a paired deep exploratory well in Kalol, screening four zones between about 253 and 308 m while its companion screens below 324 m. It belongs to a larger multi-well nest designed to compare isolated deep zones. Those zones sit in the protected confined system below 200 m.
narrative.why_it_matters: For decisions on deep groundwater, vertical separation matters: mixing shallow and deep water hides drawdown and quality risk. This nest shows where reliable deep data comes from, and why deep confined water is legally and physically constrained rather than freely expandable.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In map or 3D view look for coincident points at Khoraj Dabhi that split apart by depth — a shallow sand marker near 76-88 m versus stacked deep screens at 250-336 m — revealing the vertical testing design.

insights.title: Paired deep completions with discrete screens
insights.explanation: Records list two holes at the same site: drilled depths of 351 m and 312.5 m, completed at 341 m and 312 m. EW-II is completed with four discrete screens at 253-256 m, 271-274 m, 280-283 m and 302-308 m, while its companion is completed deeper at 324-330 m and 333-336 m.

insights.title: Part of a vertical-zone cluster
insights.explanation: Khoraj Dabhi is documented as part of a larger EWI-IV plus observation-well cluster at one village location. Like similar nests at Mahudi, Pore and Adalaj, the purpose is to isolate different vertical zones rather than test a single mixed interval.

insights.title: Deep protected aquifer with use restriction
insights.explanation: Both completion intervals lie well below 200 m, placing them in the Confined Aquifer-III 200-300 m range and deeper protected aquifers. That protected interval is restricted to drinking and domestic tapping, so these wells are investigative controls rather than models for high-volume irrigation supply.

insights.title: Different strategy from a nearby deep well
insights.explanation: A comparable deep test in Kalol taluka at Sertha was drilled to 453 m, completed at 344 m and screened continuously over 202-331 m. Khoraj Dabhi differs by using short, separated screens, which gives cleaner separation of pressures and quality by depth.

narrative.secondary_context: The shallow display interval of sand at 76-88 m covers only about the top quarter of the 351 m hole and does not represent the final deep screens. Lithology tables alone carry only depth and material with no water level, discharge or quality, and nearby Dahegam shows quality can deteriorate at depth where clays dominate.

narrative.headline: Bhat-II marks a fresh pocket in Gandhinagar's confined aquifer
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the confined zone at Bhat-II recorded 410 mg/L TDS, among the lowest values in the district survey. Nearby stations run 570-800 mg/L and northern Mansa stations reach 990-1,140 mg/L, making Bhat-II a distinctly fresher pocket in the south.
narrative.why_it_matters: Salinity differences shape how confined groundwater can be used and monitored; this fresher southern pocket stands out against the saltier trend to the north.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for the low-value point at Bhat in the south contrasting with progressively higher values toward Gandhinagar town and Mansa to the north.

insights.title: Low confined TDS at Bhat-II
insights.explanation: The May-2017 confined-aquifer sample at Bhat-II recorded 410 mg/L TDS, placing it at the low end of the district survey and indicating relatively low mineralization in the deep zone at this location.

insights.title: Fresher than surroundings, much fresher than the north
insights.explanation: Nearby Gandhinagar-II at 800 mg/L is nearly double Bhat-II, while IsanpurMota-II at 570 mg/L and Dehgam-II at 750 mg/L are also higher. Farther north, Rangpur-II at 990 mg/L and Pundhra-II at 1,140 mg/L show a strong south-to-north increase in salinity.

insights.title: Same-place contrast points to local variability
insights.explanation: A second record at the same Bhat coordinates reported 750 mg/L, well above the 410 mg/L Bhat-II value, suggesting variation between tapped zones or sampling points at the same site. A similarly low value of 430 mg/L at Dingucha-II shows Bhat-II is not isolated but part of a fresher southern pattern.

narrative.secondary_context: May 2017 confined-aquifer TDS survey across Gandhinagar, Kalol, Mansa and Dehgam talukas.

narrative.headline: Nasmed confined well shows the highest salinity recorded in Kalol in May 2017
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the confined aquifer at Nasmed recorded TDS of 3,210 mg/L, the maximum in the compiled confined dataset. Nearby confined wells in Kalol were much fresher at about 420 to 1,590 mg/L, making Nasmed a distinct high-salinity pocket.
narrative.why_it_matters: Highly mineralized deep groundwater is harder to use directly and typically needs blending, treatment or alternative sourcing. For planning, Nasmed flags localized salinity risk within an otherwise lower-TDS confined area.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In the map view look for Nasmed as an isolated high-value hotspot in southwestern Kalol, contrasting sharply with lower values to the north and east.

insights.title: Maximum confined TDS at Nasmed
insights.explanation: The confined tube well at Nasmed in Kalol taluka recorded 3210 mg/L TDS in May 2017. In the compiled table this is identified as the maximum value for the confined dataset, marking it as the saltiest deep observation in the set.

insights.title: Two to seven times saltier than neighbours
insights.explanation: Other Kalol confined stations in the same May 2017 round were markedly fresher: Dingucha-I at 1590 mg/L, Bhoyan Moti at 960 mg/L, Limbodara at 830 mg/L, Rancharada at 740 mg/L, Dingucha-II at 430 mg/L and Aluva at 420 mg/L. Nasmed is about double the next-highest and 4 to 7 times higher than most neighbours, including the sharp contrast between the two Dingucha wells at the same locality.

insights.title: Systematic pre-monsoon monitoring pinpoints a local pocket
insights.explanation: The value comes from systematic tube-well quality monitoring, with a pre-monsoon 2017 TDS map of the User Aquifer presented as the regional reference. Nasmed is located at 23.0986 N, 72.4163 E in southwestern Kalol, so its high value defines a localized mineralized pocket rather than a taluka-wide condition.

narrative.secondary_context: Pre-monsoon May 2017 snapshot of the confined User Aquifer in Gandhinagar district; values are reported TDS from tube-well monitoring.

narrative.headline: Dingucha-I shows brackish confined water next to a fresh pocket at Dingucha-II
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the Dingucha-I confined well recorded 1,590 mg/L TDS — highly mineralized water. Just beside it, Dingucha-II recorded only 430 mg/L, highlighting very sharp quality change within Kalol's confined aquifer.
narrative.why_it_matters: For any use of deep groundwater here, quality cannot be assumed from location alone: treatment needs, usability and well performance can change over tens of metres, so site-specific testing and mapping are essential.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In the map view, look for Dingucha-I as a high-TDS dot sitting almost on top of a low-TDS Dingucha-II dot — then zoom out to see Kalol swing from fresh pockets to the 3,210 mg/L high at Nasmed.

insights.title: High mineralization at this confined station
insights.explanation: The Dingucha-I confined station in Kalol taluka recorded 1,590 mg/L TDS in May 2017 pre-monsoon sampling, indicating strongly mineralized groundwater at this point.

insights.title: Extreme local and taluka-scale variability
insights.explanation: Dingucha-II, at essentially the same coordinates, recorded only 430 mg/L — nearly four times lower. Across Kalol the confined aquifer is highly patchy in the same survey, from 420 mg/L at Aluva and 830 mg/L at Limbodara to 960 mg/L at Bhoyan Moti and 3,210 mg/L at Nasmed.

insights.title: Part of regional confined-aquifer quality mapping
insights.explanation: The value comes from systematic tube-well quality monitoring by GWRDC Ltd., compiled as the pre-monsoon 2017 TDS map of the user aquifer. Dingucha-I is therefore a quality outlier to read against that mapped regional pattern, not a one-off sample.

insights.title: Nearby falling water-level signal
insights.explanation: The nearby Dingucha-II Confined Aquifer Group-II record shows a falling water-level trend over 2008-2017. Together with the high-TDS pocket at Dingucha-I, this points to a stressed, heterogeneous confined system where both quantity pressure and quality variation need joint attention.

narrative.secondary_context: Dingucha-I and Dingucha-II are listed as separate confined stations in Kalol taluka, Gandhinagar district, with near-identical lat/long around 23.33N, 72.51E.

features.location_description: Kadjodra (Thambhaliya Juna), Dehgam taluka; Y_LAT 23.17 X_LONG 72.95
features.name: Kadjodra unconfined station

narrative.headline: Kadjodra marks Dehgam's highest salinity and steepest shallow decline
narrative.summary: At Kadjodra in Dehgam taluka, the shallow unconfined aquifer recorded 1,320 mg/L TDS in May 2017 — the highest value in that month's unconfined dataset. The same station shows the steepest 2008-2017 decline at nearly 0.93 m per year, in a taluka assessed as over-exploited.
narrative.why_it_matters: Combined high salinity and persistent water-level fall signals both quality and quantity stress at one location, shaping treatment needs, yield reliability and long-term supply planning for local water use.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Kadjodra as the high point among Dehgam's shallow wells in the east — higher than nearby Hilol and Harsoli — and note its pairing of elevated salinity with a falling trend.

insights.title: Highest May-2017 shallow TDS
insights.explanation: The shallow unconfined station at Kadjodra recorded 1,320 mg/L TDS in May 2017, identified as the maximum for the unconfined dataset that month. It comes from the district's May 2017 groundwater monitoring round for the unconfined aquifer.

insights.title: Local salinity hotspot in Dehgam
insights.explanation: Nearby Dehgam shallow stations were also elevated but lower: Hilol at 1,260 mg/L and Harsoli at 890 mg/L in the same month. Kadjodra therefore stands out as a local salinity hotspot rather than an isolated high value.

insights.title: Steepest decade-long decline
insights.explanation: Trend analysis for 2008-2017 shows Kadjodra Dehgam declining at -0.9286 m/year, the most negative rate among the unconfined wells split evenly between declining and rising. It indicates persistent pre- and post-monsoon water-level fall over a decade.

insights.title: Over-exploited setting with shallower water table
insights.explanation: Dehgam's phreatic levels in May 2017 were mapped at 10-50 m below ground, placing Kadjodra in the shallower eastern-western zone. The taluka was classed as Over-Exploited in 2017, remaining Critical even after assumed micro-irrigation savings, underscoring quantity pressure alongside quality.

narrative.secondary_context: All chemistry is pre-monsoon May 2017 from the groundwater monitoring network; water-level zones and 2008-2017 trends provide seasonal and longer-term context.

features.location_description: Devkaran Na Muvada, Dehgam, Sr.1 Annexure 1 unconfined
features.name: Devkaran Na Muvada Sr.1 unconfined well

narrative.headline: Shallow village well stuck 2+ metres below its 10-year average after post-2010 drop
narrative.summary: This 19.5-m alluvial well at Devkaran Na Muvada stood at 15.2 m below ground in October 2017, about 2.2 m deeper than its 2007-2016 October average. Levels stepped sharply deeper after 2010 and have remained 13-16 m deep since 2011. A deeper 55-m well in the same village shows the same below-average pattern at even greater depth.
narrative.why_it_matters: A shallow unconfined source that stabilised at a new, deeper baseline with only a few metres of water left is more vulnerable to dry spells and local pumping. The fact that the deeper village well is also below average suggests wider aquifer stress, not just a problem with one well — relevant for water security and siting of future supply.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for the shallow marker at 82 m ground elevation with its water table down at 66.8 m — sitting well above the deeper village well's water table at 58.8 m — illustrating thin remaining saturation in the shallow alluvium.

insights.title: A clear step-down after 2010 that never recovered
insights.explanation: October levels were 8.3-10.2 m below ground from 2007-2010, then jumped to 16.1-16.2 m in 2011-2012 and have stayed in the 13.2-15.45 m range through 2017. The October 2017 level of 15.2 m is 2.24 m deeper than the 2007-2016 October average of 12.96 m, indicating a sustained downward step rather than a single dry year.

insights.title: Very little water left in a very shallow hole
insights.explanation: The hole is only 19.5 m deep with ground elevation at 82 m, so 15.2 m of depth-to-water in October 2017 leaves about 4.3 m of saturated section in the well and a calculated water-table elevation of 66.8 m above sea level. For a shallow unconfined well, that thin remaining water column makes it sensitive to further late-season declines.

insights.title: Deeper neighbour confirms the village-wide weakness
insights.explanation: A second unconfined well in the same village, drilled to 55 m, stood at 23.2 m below ground in October 2017 versus its own decadal average of 21.66 m, also below average. Its water-table elevation of 58.8 m is 8 m lower than the shallow well's 66.8 m, showing deeper groundwater in the same alluvium is also under pressure.

insights.title: Shallow alluvium explains the volatility
insights.explanation: Both village wells are logged as ALV geology and unconfined aquifer, meaning they tap shallow alluvial sediments that typically respond quickly to recharge and pumping. That setting helps explain the sharp post-2010 shift and the persistence of deeper levels in this monitoring record.

narrative.secondary_context: October post-monsoon monitoring in Dehgam taluk, part of the Annexure 1 unconfined water-level network comparing 2017 to 2007-2016 averages.

narrative.headline: Palaiya's 17-m Shallow Well Hit Its Deepest Level on Record
narrative.summary: This 17-m-deep unconfined well at Palaiya recorded water at 15.3 m depth in October 2017, about 3.7 m deeper than its 10-year average and the deepest in its 2007-2017 record. With less than 2 m of water remaining above the bottom of the hole, the shallow alluvial aquifer here looks acutely stressed.
narrative.why_it_matters: A record-low level in such a shallow well is an early warning for local supply reliability: further decline could leave the well dry and signals that recharge is not keeping pace with demand in this pocket of Dehgam.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In map and 3D view, look for a very short well stick at Palaiya with the water mark sitting almost at the bottom — unlike deeper wells nearby that still have storage above their base.

insights.title: October 2017 level at 15.3 m depth
insights.explanation: In October 2017 the depth to water was 15.3 m below ground level, corresponding to a water-table elevation of 61.7 m where ground elevation is 77 m. The table schema confirms these columns are October water level and calculated water table.

insights.title: 3.69 m below average after sharp late decline
insights.explanation: The 2017 level was 3.69 m deeper than the 2007-2016 decadal average of 11.61 m. The full October series rose from 9.4 m in 2007 and 9.75 m in 2014 to 12.25 m in 2015, 14.65 m in 2016 and 15.3 m in 2017, making 2017 the deepest in the 11-year record with most of the fall in the last two years.

insights.title: Only about 1.7 m of water left in the well
insights.explanation: The well is drilled to only 17 m, so a 15.3 m water level leaves about 1.7 m of water column in the hole. For a shallow monitoring well this thin remaining saturation signals the well is close to its bottom and highly sensitive to further decline.

insights.title: Shallow alluvial unconfined aquifer
insights.explanation: The station is listed as an unconfined alluvium (ALV) well at Palaiya, Dehgam, with ground elevation 77 m. That shallow alluvial unconfined setting typically responds quickly to recharge and pumping, which helps explain the large year-to-year swings seen here.

narrative.secondary_context: Part of the Annexure 1 unconfined October monitoring network comparing October 2007-2016 to October 2017.

narrative.headline: Harsoli well breaks five-year stability with sharp 2017 drop
narrative.summary: This 90-metre unconfined well in alluvium at Harsoli held between 43.9 and 45.1 m depth from 2012 to 2016, then deepened to 48.3 m in October 2017, 3.8 m below its average. The drop leaves the water table at just 14.7 m, very low for ground at 63 m.
narrative.why_it_matters: A stable shallow-alluvium record that suddenly deepens points to increased lift, pumping effort and vulnerability to another weak recharge season. For planning, this is a watch-point for whether 2017 was a one-year dip or the start of a declining trend.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In map and 3D view, look for a deep water marker far below the 63-m ground surface and a low water-table surface — the break from a flat five-year line to a sharp 2017 low is the signal to notice.

insights.title: Five stable years then a sudden deepening
insights.explanation: October levels were 44.6 m in 2012, 45.1 m in 2013, 44.0 m in 2014, 43.9 m in 2015 and 44.9 m in 2016 — a tight 1.2 m band — then deepened to 48.3 m in October 2017, about 3.4 m deeper than the prior year.

insights.title: Deep level leaves a very low water table
insights.explanation: October 2017 depth of 48.3 m is 3.8 m deeper than the 44.5 m average, recorded as a -3.8 m fluctuation. With ground at 63 m, this leaves the calculated water table at only 14.7 m.

insights.title: 90-m alluvial unconfined setting
insights.explanation: The well is 90 m deep in alluvium and classified as unconfined, with levels reported in the unconfined October 2007-2016 plus October 2017 table structure. More than half the drilled depth is now unsaturated, with water encountered only below about 48 m.

narrative.secondary_context: The labelled decadal average is effectively a 2012-2016 five-year average because 2007-2011 cells are empty, so treat the -3.8 m comparison as short-record rather than a full 10-year baseline.

narrative.headline: Hilol well is holding above its decade average after a sharp recovery from 2012 lows
narrative.summary: At Hilol, Dehgam, groundwater was 32.25 m below ground in October 2017, about 1.37 m shallower than the decadal average of 33.62 m. The record shows a strong rebound from 39.6 m in 2012 into a 30-33 m band through 2017, indicating stabilization rather than continued decline in this 90 m alluvial unconfined well.
narrative.why_it_matters: For decisions around shallow supply and recharge, Hilol signals resilience: despite year-to-year swings of several metres, the aquifer has not reverted to 2012 depths. It is a useful watch point for whether that recovered band holds under future dry seasons and pumping.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In the map and 3D view, look for a deep unconfined point near 62 m ground elevation with the water table near 30 m — a recovered lowland pocket rather than a shallow water-table high.

insights.title: Deep but stable unconfined level in 2017
insights.explanation: In October 2017 water was 32.25 m below ground in this 90 m-deep unconfined well, with ground at 62 m leaving a water-table elevation of about 29.75 m. That depth is the core signal for storage in the shallow alluvium at Hilol, Dehgam.

insights.title: Recovery and recent variability
insights.explanation: October 2017 was 1.37 m shallower than the decadal average of 33.62 m, where positive fluctuation means shallower than average. The yearly record shows why: 39.6 m in 2012, then 33.5 m in 2013, 32.1 m in 2014, 33.0 m in 2015, 29.9 m in 2016 and 32.25 m in 2017 — a step recovery after 2012 followed by 2-3 m year-to-year swings.

insights.title: Alluvial unconfined setting
insights.explanation: Hilol is completed in alluvium (ALV) and listed as unconfined, the same setting as the Adalaj monitoring well, but Hilol is much deeper to water and has a larger positive deviation from average. Both wells show 2017 shallower than average, making Hilol the deeper, more variable example of an alluvial unconfined response.

narrative.secondary_context: Part of the October unconfined-aquifer monitoring round comparing October 2017 to an October 2007-2016 decadal average.

narrative.headline: Kadjodra well drops sharply in 2017 to near the bottom of the hole
narrative.summary: In October 2017 water at Kadjodra stood 45.8 m below ground, about 8.3 m deeper than its 37.54 m decadal average after five years near 36-39 m. With a drilled depth of only 48 m, barely 2 m of water column remained, marking the largest fall in this data group.
narrative.why_it_matters: A sudden drop to near total depth in a shallow unconfined alluvial well signals local supply stress, higher pumping lift and vulnerability to another poor recharge season, making it a priority spot to watch for reliability.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for a deep outlier at Kadjodra in Dehgam — a near-bottom water level where the water column is almost gone compared with steadier nearby alluvial wells.

insights.title: Stable for years, then a sudden deepening
insights.explanation: October levels held between 36.4 m and 39.25 m from 2012 to 2016, then jumped to 45.8 m in October 2017 — a one-year deepening of about 6.5 m. The decadal average is 37.54 m, giving a fluctuation of -8.26 m, described as the largest fall in this group.

insights.title: Well left with very little saturated thickness
insights.explanation: Ground level is 83 m with a drilled depth of 48 m, while water was at 45.8 m below ground in October 2017. That leaves only about 2.2 m above the drilled bottom, with a calculated water-table elevation of 37.2 m.

insights.title: A local outlier, not a uniform decline
insights.explanation: Kadjodra's -8.26 m fluctuation contrasts with a nearby alluvial unconfined record at Adalaj that was essentially stable at +0.39 m in 2017 versus its average. This makes Kadjodra an outlier for depletion rather than part of a uniform regional shift.

insights.title: Shallow alluvial unconfined setting
insights.explanation: The well is completed in alluvium (ALV) and listed as unconfined at Kadjodra, Dehgam. The table compares October 2007-2016 history and decadal average against October 2017 to derive fluctuation and water table.

narrative.secondary_context: Part of the Annexure 1 unconfined October water-level network; water table is ground elevation minus 2017 depth (83 - 45.8 = 37.2).

narrative.headline: Rakhiyal well stabilized after sharp early-2010s recovery
narrative.summary: In October 2017 the Rakhiyal unconfined well stood at 33.75 m below ground, 1.74 m shallower than its decadal average. After a deep 40.2 m low in 2012, levels recovered by 2014 and have since held steady around 33-34 m.
narrative.why_it_matters: Holding above the long-term average after recovery suggests near-term stability for local supply, but the absolute depth near 34 m still means significant pumping lift and continued dependence on sustained recharge.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for a 60-m alluvial well on high ground at 96 m elevation with the water table near 62 m — a flat recent line after a steep climb from the 2012 low.

insights.title: Deep but measurable water level in 2017
insights.explanation: In October 2017 depth to water was 33.75 m below ground in this 60-m-deep well, corresponding to a water-table elevation of 62.25 m from 96 m ground level. That leaves roughly half the drilled depth water-bearing at the time of measurement.

insights.title: 2012-2014 recovery, then flat through 2017
insights.explanation: October levels improved from 40.2 m in 2012 to 36.5 m in 2013 to 33.4 m in 2014, then stayed within 33.4-33.8 m through 2015-2017. The pattern is a rapid 6-7 m recovery followed by three years of stability rather than continued rise or decline.

insights.title: Above decadal average
insights.explanation: The decadal average depth is 35.49 m, so the 2017 level at 33.75 m is 1.74 m shallower than average. A positive fluctuation here means better-than-average conditions, confirming the recent stable period is holding above the long-term mean.

insights.title: Unconfined alluvial setting
insights.explanation: The well is recorded as an unconfined monitoring point in alluvium at Rakhiyal, Dehgam. In this setting, the post-2012 rebound and subsequent flat trend is consistent with an alluvial water table responding to recharge and then equilibrating, which is what to watch in the map and 3D view.

features.location_description: Patna Kuva, Dehgam, Sr.7 Annexure 1 unconfined
features.name: Patna Kuva Sr.7 unconfined well

narrative.headline: Deep unconfined level at Patna Kuva, but 2017 was its shallowest in six years
narrative.summary: The Patna Kuva unconfined well had October 2017 water 62.5 m below ground, about 2.2 m shallower than its 64.68 m decadal average. The 2012-2017 series stayed deep between about 63.7 and 65.3 m before dropping to that 6-year high in 2017, with water-table elevation at 38.5 m.
narrative.why_it_matters: A 60-m-plus lift implies higher pumping energy and vulnerability if levels fall again, so the 2017 rebound matters: it shows this deep alluvial zone can still respond upward, but the baseline remains exceptionally deep for an unconfined well.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In map or 3D view look for a tall unsaturated column down to ~62 m at Patna Kuva, contrasting with much shallower water nearby, and a small upward step in 2017 after several flat deep years.

insights.title: A very deep unconfined water level
insights.explanation: In October 2017 water stood 62.5 m below ground in a 90-m-deep well drilled in ALV material at 101 m ground elevation, leaving a calculated water-table elevation of 38.5 m. That depth leaves only about 27.5 m of saturated thickness above the bottom of the hole.

insights.title: Stable-deep record with a 2017 recovery
insights.explanation: October levels were 65.3 m in 2012, 64.8 m in 2013, 63.7 m in 2014, 64.7 m in 2015, 64.9 m in 2016 and then 62.5 m in 2017, against a decadal average of 64.68 m. The reported fluctuation of 2.18 m therefore represents water about 2.2 m shallower, or higher, than average.

insights.title: Much deeper than neighbouring Dehgam wells
insights.explanation: The nearby Dehgam record at Devkaran Na Muvada stood at only 15.2 m depth in October 2017 with a water-table elevation of 66.8 m, versus 62.5 m depth and 38.5 m elevation at Patna Kuva. Patna Kuva is therefore an outlier for depth to water even though both are listed as unconfined wells in ALV geology.

insights.title: What the monitoring record represents
insights.explanation: This site belongs to the October unconfined monitoring table that preserves yearly October 2007-2016 levels, a decadal average, October 2017 level, fluctuation and derived water table. The pre-2012 yearly cells are empty for Patna Kuva, so its average effectively reflects the 2012-2016 period.

narrative.secondary_context: Part of the Annexure-1 unconfined October network; a separate Annexure-2 network tracks confined Aquifer-I levels for May 2017.

narrative.headline: A deep alluvial well holding steady just above its 10-year average
narrative.summary: In October 2017 water stood 34.7 m below ground in this 60-m alluvial well, about 1.1 m shallower than its decadal average of 35.8 m. The 2012-2017 record swung from 38.0 m to 33.2 m before settling near 34.7 m, placing the water table near 45.3 m above sea level.
narrative.why_it_matters: Stability near the long-term mean matters more than the single 1.1-m uptick: it suggests this pocket of unconfined alluvium is not in sharp decline, but the absolute depth still implies high lift and sensitivity to dry-year drops.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In map or 3D view look for a tall dry column down to about 35 m in a 60-m hole on 80-m ground, with the water surface near 45 m elevation after earlier ups and downs.

insights.title: October 2017 level versus long-term mean
insights.explanation: October 2017 depth was 34.7 m below ground compared with a decadal average of 35.8 m, giving a +1.1 m fluctuation. Positive here means shallower than average — a modest recovery, not a deepening.

insights.title: 2012-2017 swing then stabilization
insights.explanation: October readings ran 37.3 m in 2012, 38.0 m in 2013, 35.7 m in 2014, 33.2 m in 2015, 34.8 m in 2016 and 34.7 m in 2017. The pattern is a 4-5 m swing up and then two years of near-flat levels around 34.7-34.8 m.

insights.title: Alluvial unconfined setting
insights.explanation: The well is 60 m deep in mapped alluvium and classified as unconfined, with ground at 80 m. The reported water table of 45.3 m is ground elevation minus October depth, the standard derivation for this October monitoring table.

narrative.secondary_context: Part of the Annexure 1 unconfined October monitoring set where decadal average covers October 2007-2016 and water table is ground elevation minus October depth.

narrative.headline: Deeper village well runs below its 10-year average
narrative.summary: In October 2017 water stood 23.2 m below ground in this 55-m unconfined alluvial well, about 1.5 m deeper than its 2007-2016 October average of 21.66 m. The implied water table at 58.8 m sits about 8 m below a shallower village well at the same ground elevation, marking this as the low-water end-member locally.
narrative.why_it_matters: A level that remains below its 10-year mean after climbing from ~18 m to ~23 m implies tighter storage and higher lift than earlier in the record. For investment or supply planning, expect higher pumping effort and less drought buffer here than the shallow village level suggests.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In map and 3D view look for two very close village wells at the same 82-m surface: this deeper well with water near 59 m elevation, sitting visibly lower than its 19.5-m neighbour at about 67 m.

insights.title: October 2017 level and water-table position
insights.explanation: In October 2017 water stood 23.2 m below ground in this 55-m-deep well. With ground at 82 m, that puts the water table at 58.8 m, leaving about 31.8 m of saturated section above the drilled bottom.

insights.title: Below-average after a decade of deepening
insights.explanation: The 2017 level is 1.54 m deeper than the October 2007-2016 average of 21.66 m. The 10-year October series rose from 17.8 m in 2007 to 23-24.5 m after 2010 and stayed high at 23.2 m in 2017, showing persistent deepening rather than a one-year dip.

insights.title: 8 m lower than the shallow neighbour
insights.explanation: A second unconfined alluvial well in the same village at the same 82-m ground level is only 19.5 m deep and stood at 15.2 m in October 2017, with a water table at 66.8 m. This 55-m well is about 8 m deeper to water and 8 m lower in water-table elevation, and both wells were below their decadal averages in 2017.

insights.title: Same alluvial aquifer, deeper access point
insights.explanation: Both village wells are in alluvium and tap the unconfined aquifer. The contrast is construction depth, 55 m versus 19.5 m, not geology or surface elevation, making this well the deeper sampler of the same shallow system.

narrative.headline: Jindva well dropped ~8 m then stuck below average
narrative.summary: In October 2017 water stood 36.3 m below ground at Jindva, 2.55 m deeper than its 10-year October average. Levels deepened by about 8 m between 2007 and 2012 and have since flattened near 36 m, leaving the water table at about 51.7 m elevation.
narrative.why_it_matters: A stabilized but below-average level suggests the aquifer stopped falling but has not refilled, which matters for pumping depth, dry-season availability, and whether future monsoons or demand changes shift the plateau up or down.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for a deep-level point with a low water-table surface well below the 88 m ground surface, and a time curve that slopes down steeply to 2012 then goes flat.

insights.title: Early fall, then flat near 36 m
insights.explanation: October depth went from 28.5 m in 2007 and 28.45 m in 2008 to 32.2 m in 2009, 33.15 m in 2010, 35.2 m in 2011 and 36.2 m in 2012, then held at 35.7-36.3 m through 2017. The pattern is an early multi-year deepening followed by a 5-year plateau near 36 m rather than a single-year dip.

insights.title: 2017 sits 2.55 m below decadal norm
insights.explanation: October 2017 depth was 36.3 m below ground versus a 2007-2016 October average of 33.75 m, giving a fluctuation of -2.55 m where negative means deeper than average. Ground at 88 m minus 36.3 m puts the water-table surface at 51.7 m.

insights.title: Deep alluvial well with no rebound
insights.explanation: Jindva is completed in alluvium as an unconfined well drilled to 63.41 m, so 36.3 m of drawdown still leaves water in the lower hole. Unlike the Adalaj alluvium record at 23.45 m in 2017 and 0.39 m above its average, Jindva remains below its average, showing no matching recovery.

narrative.secondary_context: Unconfined alluvium post-monsoon October series, 2007-2017, Dehgam area.

features.location_description: Dingucha-II, Kalol; elev 84 m; 23.33, 72.51; depth 240 m
features.name: Dingucha-II Confined-II

narrative.headline: Dingucha-II deep well: steepest pressure fall in Kalol, but notably fresher water
narrative.summary: Dingucha-II's deep Confined Group-II well recorded the steepest 2008-2017 pressure decline among nearby Kalol stations. Yet its pre-monsoon 2017 water remains relatively fresh at 430 TDS, far lower than 1,590 next door at Dingucha-I. It is a quantitatively stressed but qualitatively favorable pocket.
narrative.why_it_matters: For decisions, the fresh quality is an advantage, but the fastest local decline signals rising pumping lift, higher energy cost and long-term sustainability risk if the trend continues. The extreme neighbor contrast also warns that quality cannot be assumed by proximity alone.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In the map and 3D view, look for Dingucha-II as a deep low-TDS point inside a cluster of falling-level wells — color for fresh quality against downward arrows for pressure.

insights.title: Sustained decade-long decline
insights.explanation: From 2008-2017 the Confined Aquifer Group-II at Dingucha-II trends downward at -1.74 per year, classified as Fall. That marks sustained loss of pressure head in this 240-m deep confined zone, not a single-season dip.

insights.title: Part of a wider Kalol decline
insights.explanation: Nearby Group-II stations in Kalol show the same pattern: Bhoyan Moti, Rancharada and Chhatral all falling, while only Kalol replacement piezometer shows a small rise. Dingucha-II is the steepest faller in this cluster, indicating area-wide stress rather than an isolated well problem.

insights.title: Fresh pocket next to saline water
insights.explanation: Pre-monsoon 2017 confined water at Dingucha-II measured 430 TDS versus 1590 TDS at Dingucha-I at essentially the same location. The sharp contrast shows good-quality water can sit very close to much more mineralized water, suggesting strong local compartmentalization.

insights.title: Monitored, comparable quality snapshot
insights.explanation: These values come from systematic tube-well monitoring of the user aquifer with a pre-monsoon 2017 TDS map. The quality contrast is therefore comparable across stations and useful for siting and risk screening.

narrative.secondary_context: Deep Confined Aquifer Group-II monitoring point in Kalol tahsil, tracked for both water-level trend and pre-monsoon quality as part of the confined-aquifer assessment.

narrative.headline: Gandhinagar's deep aquifer runs saltier than its closest neighbors
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the confined well at Gandhinagar-II recorded 800 mg/L total dissolved solids. That is nearly double nearby fresher wells at Bhat-II and Dingucha-II around 410-430 mg/L, but below the most mineralized northern wells above 990 mg/L. The reading comes from the regional pre-monsoon survey of deep used aquifers.
narrative.why_it_matters: Dissolved solids track overall saltiness and how much treatment or blending a water source may need — this mid-to-high value shows usable deep water here is saltier than the best local sources, making short-distance quality differences a key factor in siting and planning.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Gandhinagar-II as a mid-range point between fresher dots to the south and west and higher-salinity dots to the north in Mansa.

insights.title: 800 mg/L dissolved solids at this deep well
insights.explanation: The tube well assigned to the confined aquifer at Gandhinagar-II recorded 800 mg/L total dissolved solids in the May 2017 pre-monsoon sampling, defining this location as moderately mineralized deep groundwater.

insights.title: Mid-point in a sharp local salinity gradient
insights.explanation: Nearby wells in the same confined survey are much fresher to the south and west — Bhat-II at 410 mg/L, Dingucha-II at 430 mg/L and IsanpurMota-II at 570 mg/L — and similar at Dehgam-II at 750 mg/L, while wells to the north in Mansa taluka climb to 990 mg/L at Rangpur-II and 1,140 mg/L at Pundhra-II. Gandhinagar-II therefore marks a middle step in a strong south-to-north increase in salinity over a short distance.

insights.title: Part of systematic deep-aquifer quality mapping
insights.explanation: This value is not an isolated test but part of systematic monitoring of tube wells by GWRDC Ltd., compiled as a pre-monsoon 2017 map of dissolved solids in the used confined aquifer. It allows like-for-like comparison of deep-aquifer quality across the district.

narrative.secondary_context: Single pre-monsoon snapshot from May 2017; shows spatial pattern, not a time trend.

narrative.headline: A fresh-water pocket in a declining deep aquifer — next to a salty twin well
narrative.summary: At Dingucha-II in Kalol, the deep confined aquifer measured 430 mg/L TDS in May 2017, while the virtually co-located Dingucha-I well measured 1,590 mg/L. At the same time, 2008-2017 monitoring for Confined Aquifer Group-II shows water levels falling at Dingucha-II, in line with most nearby Kalol wells.
narrative.why_it_matters: The fresh quality makes this spot stand out for deep-aquifer use, but the falling trend and the metre-scale quality jump show the resource is both stressed and compartmentalized — quality and performance cannot be extrapolated from neighbours and need zone-specific testing and level monitoring.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Dingucha-II as a low-TDS point sitting almost on top of high-TDS Dingucha-I in Kalol — a fresh spot inside a cluster where deep levels have mostly been falling.

insights.title: Relatively fresh confined water in May 2017
insights.explanation: Pre-monsoon 2017 sampling of the confined tube-well network recorded 430 mg/L TDS at Dingucha-II in Kalol taluka. That is a direct measured value for the deep, confined system, not an estimate.

insights.title: Sharp contrast with co-located Dingucha-I
insights.explanation: The virtually co-located Dingucha-I station recorded 1,590 mg/L at the same time — nearly four times higher. Such a sharp difference over essentially the same map location points to vertical separation or compartmentalization between tapped zones, not a uniform aquifer.

insights.title: Decade-long decline in the deep aquifer
insights.explanation: For Confined Aquifer Group-II, the 2008-2017 record at Dingucha-II is classified as Fall with a reported value of -1.74429. In other words, water levels/pressures were on a sustained downward path over that decade despite the good quality snapshot in 2017.

insights.title: Part of a wider Kalol decline
insights.explanation: Nearby Kalol Group-II stations at Bhoyan Moti, Rancharada and Chhatral also show Fall over 2008-2017, confirming Dingucha-II is part of a wider stressed pocket. The Kalol replacement piezometer is the local exception with a Rise, underscoring that trends vary by zone and well.

narrative.headline: Limbodara's deep water shows mid-range salinity in a patchy Kalol aquifer
narrative.summary: In May 2017, the confined tube well at Limbodara in Kalol taluka recorded total dissolved solids of 830 mg/L. That places it in the middle of nearby deep-well results, which range from about 420 mg/L to over 3,000 mg/L, highlighting sharp local differences in the same aquifer.
narrative.why_it_matters: For planning that depends on deep groundwater, Limbodara looks more workable than the most saline pockets nearby, but the wide swings within a short distance mean water quality cannot be assumed from one village to the next — each site needs its own check.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Limbodara as a mid-tone point among Kalol's confined wells — lower than Nasmed and Dingucha-I to the southwest, but higher than nearby fresher points like Aluva and Dingucha-II.

insights.title: 830 mg/L in Limbodara confined well
insights.explanation: A direct sample from the confined tube well at Limbodara, Kalol taluka, recorded 830 mg/L total dissolved solids in May 2017 pre-monsoon conditions.

insights.title: Mid-range amid sharp local contrasts
insights.explanation: Nearby confined wells in the same taluka range widely: Nasmed at 3,210 mg/L and Dingucha-I at 1,590 mg/L are much higher, while Bhoyan Moti at 960 mg/L and Rancharada at 740 mg/L are close, and Dingucha-II at 430 mg/L and Aluva at 420 mg/L are much lower. Limbodara sits in the middle, showing that salinity changes sharply over short distances in this aquifer.

insights.title: Part of district-wide pre-monsoon survey
insights.explanation: The result comes from systematic monitoring of tube-well quality by GWRDC Ltd., compiled as a pre-monsoon 2017 map of TDS in the used confined aquifer, so it is a seasonal snapshot designed for area-to-area comparison.

narrative.headline: Pundhra-I is a saltier pocket in Mansa's confined aquifer
narrative.summary: In May 2017, confined groundwater at Pundhra-I in Mansa measured 1300 mg/L TDS. It is saltier than neighboring confined wells in Kharna, Rangpur and nearby Pundhra-II, but remains within the report's largely potable range below 2000 mg/L.
narrative.why_it_matters: It signals that deep groundwater here is usable but saltier than surroundings, so users relying on this confined source should expect more mineralized water and plan for blending, treatment choice, and monitoring of any further westward deterioration.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Pundhra-I as a relatively higher-value point among the lower Mansa cluster — darker than Kharna and Rangpur to help spot local salinity variation.

insights.title: Confined-aquifer salinity measurement
insights.explanation: Pre-monsoon 2017 monitoring of the confined tube well at Pundhra-I recorded total dissolved solids of 1300 mg/L. It comes from the systematic tube-well quality monitoring program used to map the used confined aquifer.

insights.title: Higher than nearby Mansa wells
insights.explanation: Pundhra-I at 1300 mg/L is higher than its immediate neighbor Pundhra-II at 1140 mg/L and distinctly higher than other Mansa confined stations such as Kharna-I at 780 mg/L, Kharna-III at 660 mg/L, Rangpur-I at 740 mg/L and Rangpur-II at 990 mg/L. This makes Pundhra-I stand out locally as a higher-salinity point.

insights.title: Fits regional east-to-west pattern
insights.explanation: Across the confined system, salinity ranges from about 500 mg/L to over 2700 mg/L and generally deteriorates from east to west in the direction of groundwater flow, with the highest values around Chhatral in the west. Pundhra-I at 1300 mg/L sits within the major potable portion below 2000 mg/L, not in the extreme western high-salinity zone.

narrative.headline: Pundhra-II shows salty confined water but a rising water level
narrative.summary: Pundhra-II in Mansa recorded 1,140 mg/L TDS in the confined aquifer in May 2017 — brackish and near the top of local values. Unusually, its Confined Group-II water level trended upward from 2008-2017, diverging from declining sites like Kharna-III.
narrative.why_it_matters: Salinity at this level raises treatment and usability costs even where the aquifer is marked suitable for drinking and irrigation, while the rising level suggests quantity stress is easing locally — a divide that matters for siting, blending, and treatment planning.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for the tight Pundhra-I and Pundhra-II pair lighting up as a high-salinity spot, with levels recovering underneath — salinity and quantity moving in opposite directions.

insights.title: Brackish confined-water measurement
insights.explanation: A pre-monsoon 2017 sample from the confined system at Pundhra-II measured 1,140 mg/L total dissolved solids. It comes from the district tube-well quality monitoring used to map the user aquifer, so it represents deeper confined groundwater rather than a shallow dug-well snapshot.

insights.title: Higher than its immediate neighbours
insights.explanation: Very close by, Pundhra-I measured higher at 1,300 mg/L while Rangpur-II to the southeast measured lower at 990 mg/L. That pattern points to a localized higher-salinity pocket around Pundhra rather than a uniform taluka-wide value.

insights.title: Water level rising while quality stays brackish
insights.explanation: For Confined Aquifer Group-II over 2008-2017, the Pundhara-II station shows a rising trend of about 0.45, while Kharna-III in the same group and taluka shows a falling trend. In other words, water quantity pressure is improving here even though salinity remains elevated.

insights.title: Deep stacked aquifer setting
insights.explanation: In Mansa, the confined system is stacked: Confined I at 100-150 m, Confined II at 185-210 m and Confined III at 260-300 m below ground, above a 0-70 m phreatic zone. Pundhra is one of the repeat -I/-II paired monitoring villages, designed to track differences within the same area across this stacked system.

narrative.secondary_context: One of 6 Mansa monitoring stations in a 30-station district network for pre-monsoon 2017 confined-aquifer TDS mapping.

features.location_description: Indroda, Gandhinagar taluka; lat truncated to 23.2
features.name: Indroda

narrative.headline: Indroda's confined water is notably fresh in a patchy salinity landscape
narrative.summary: Indroda's confined aquifer measured 430 mg/L TDS in May 2017, among the freshest results in the Gandhinagar monitoring set. Neighbouring wells range from similar lows to over 3,000 mg/L, showing sharp local variability in deeper groundwater quality.
narrative.why_it_matters: Lower salinity in the confined system means less mineral load to manage for sustained use, making Indroda a relatively favorable reference point. The sharp differences nearby mean future planning cannot assume this freshness extends uniformly — it needs well-by-well checking.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Find the low-value point at Indroda and compare it to higher-value neighbours to the north and west — the contrast highlights a fresher pocket within a variable confined aquifer.

insights.title: 430 mg/L TDS in confined aquifer
insights.explanation: A pre-monsoon May 2017 sample from the confined aquifer at Indroda measured 430 mg/L TDS. Coordinates for this record are truncated, so treat the map point as approximate rather than exact.

insights.title: Among the lowest values locally
insights.explanation: Indroda sits at the fresh end alongside Bhat-II at 410 mg/L and Dingucha-II at 430 mg/L, while nearby wells are distinctly more mineralized: Gandhinagar-II at 800 mg/L, Limbodara at 830 mg/L, Dingucha-I at 1,590 mg/L and Nasmed at 3,210 mg/L. The more than seven-fold range over short distances shows salinity is highly localized, not a uniform background.

insights.title: Part of systematic confined-aquifer monitoring
insights.explanation: This value comes from GWRDC Ltd. tube-well monitoring, compiled into a pre-monsoon 2017 TDS map of the User Aquifer. Use Indroda as one monitored control point for that deeper confined system, not as a picture of shallow groundwater.

narrative.headline: Mid-range salinity but falling levels in Bhoyan Moti's confined aquifer
narrative.summary: The confined well at Bhoyan Moti recorded 960 mg/L dissolved solids in May 2017, mid-range among nearby Kalol confined wells that span 430 to 3,210 mg/L. The same station shows a falling signal for Confined Aquifer Group-II over 2008-2017, indicating the deeper resource is under pressure despite its moderate salinity.
narrative.why_it_matters: For decisions, this is a quantity-plus-quality signal: the water is less saline than several neighbours, but persistent decline means future availability and pumping effort depend on managing withdrawals and tracking quality together.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Find Bhoyan Moti in southern Kalol: its colour will sit between fresher spots like Dingucha-II and strong high-salinity spots like Nasmed, while its 2008-2017 trace trends downward.

insights.title: 960 mg/L in the confined aquifer
insights.explanation: A pre-monsoon May 2017 sample from the confined aquifer at Bhoyan Moti, Kalol taluka, recorded 960 mg/L total dissolved solids. It is a direct monitored value for the deeper, confined system rather than shallow groundwater.

insights.title: Falling trend over 2008-2017
insights.explanation: The same station, assigned to Confined Aquifer Group-II, carries a reported trend value of -1.50286 with a Fall direction for 2008-2017. In other words, water levels were declining over the decade even where salinity was not extreme.

insights.title: Middle of a highly variable neighbourhood
insights.explanation: Bhoyan Moti sits in the middle locally: higher than Limbodara at 830 mg/L and Dingucha-II at 430 mg/L, lower than Adraj Moti at 1,160 mg/L, Dingucha-I at 1,590 mg/L, and Nasmed at 3,210 mg/L. The very large spread among Kalol confined wells, including two very different values at Dingucha, points to a patchy deeper aquifer rather than uniform quality.

insights.title: Part of systematic confined-aquifer mapping
insights.explanation: The value comes from the GWRDC tube-well monitoring programme, whose pre-monsoon 2017 TDS map for the used confined aquifer is presented as Fig.18. This gives confidence it is part of a systematic regional snapshot, not an isolated test.

narrative.headline: Fresher confined water at Isanpur Mota-I, but neighbours vary sharply
narrative.summary: This monitoring station recorded 440 mg/L TDS in the confined aquifer in May 2017, placing it at the fresher end of the district network. Two co-located Isanpur Mota wells read notably higher at 570 and 820 mg/L, so quality cannot be assumed uniform even within this site.
narrative.why_it_matters: Lower mineralization here implies lower treatment burden and better suitability for use than many nearby confined sources, but the sharp on-site variation means any new supply well needs its own quality test and continued monitoring.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for a low-value point at Isanpur Mota-I surrounded by higher values at the same location and to the west — a local freshness anomaly in a variable TDS field.

insights.title: 440 mg/L confined TDS at this station
insights.explanation: This tube well recorded 440 mg/L TDS in the confined aquifer in the pre-monsoon May 2017 round. It is part of the GWRDC tube-well network used to map TDS of the used aquifer in 2017.

insights.title: Same village, very different readings
insights.explanation: Two companion wells at essentially the same coordinates recorded 570 mg/L and 820 mg/L: Isanpur Mota-II and III versus 440 mg/L at Isanpur Mota-I. That ~380 mg/L spread at one village points to strong well-to-well variability rather than uniform quality across the site.

insights.title: At the fresher end of the district snapshot
insights.explanation: In the district snapshot, this 440 mg/L value sits with the fresher group alongside Bhat-II at 410 mg/L and Dingucha-II at 430 mg/L. It contrasts with higher confined readings such as 800 mg/L at Gandhinagar-II and 1,590 mg/L at Dingucha-I, showing the district spans fresh to distinctly mineralized water.

narrative.secondary_context: Pre-monsoon May 2017 confined-aquifer TDS survey across Gandhinagar district tube wells.

narrative.headline: Medra: freshest confined-aquifer reading in the May 2017 round
narrative.summary: In May 2017, the confined well at Medra recorded 400 mg/L total dissolved solids — the lowest value in this district subset. It was collected as part of the regional pre-monsoon survey of the deeper User Aquifer. Nearby wells show the same aquifer can be much saltier, making Medra a fresh-water end-member.
narrative.why_it_matters: Medra identifies where the deep confined system is freshest before the monsoon, amid variations up to more than 3,000 mg/L nearby. That contrast matters for prioritizing this pocket for protection and for understanding that deep water quality cannot be assumed uniform across short distances.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Medra in Gandhinagar taluka as a low-TDS point clustering with Bhat-II near 410 mg/L, standing out sharply against higher-salinity points to the west and north such as Nasmed and Dingucha-I.

insights.title: Lowest May 2017 confined TDS at 400 mg/L
insights.explanation: The confined tube well at Medra recorded 400 mg/L total dissolved solids in May 2017. This is identified as the confined minimum in the supplied set and represents relatively fresh, low-mineralization deep groundwater for the pre-monsoon period.

insights.title: Sharp contrast with saltier wells in same network
insights.explanation: Medra at 400 mg/L clusters with nearby fresh points Bhat-II at 410 mg/L and Dingucha-II at 430 mg/L. The same confined network is much saltier elsewhere: Gandhinagar-II at 800 mg/L and Limbodara at 830 mg/L are about double, Dingucha-I at 1590 mg/L is about four times higher, and Nasmed at 3210 mg/L is about eight times higher, showing strong spatial variability in the deep aquifer.

insights.title: Part of systematic pre-monsoon User Aquifer survey
insights.explanation: This value comes from systematic monitoring of tube-well groundwater quality, with a pre-monsoon 2017 map of TDS in the User Aquifer presented as Fig. 18. Medra should therefore be read as one point in a regional confined-aquifer snapshot, not an isolated test.

insights.title: Location is approximate
insights.explanation: The Medra coordinate is flagged as low, truncated latitude precision in Gandhinagar taluka. Treat its map position as approximate when comparing to neighboring wells, while the taluka-level pattern of a fresh pocket remains clear.

features.location_description: Unava, Gandhinagar taluka; lat 24.3675 outlier to verify
features.name: Unava

narrative.headline: Moderate deep-well salinity, but mapped far north of its district cluster
narrative.summary: The Unava confined well measured 710 mg/L TDS in May 2017 — moderate compared with 410 to 3210 mg/L elsewhere in Gandhinagar. Its listed latitude of 24.3675°N places it far north of all peer stations and is flagged for verification.
narrative.why_it_matters: For decisions, the chemistry suggests a less-saline deep aquifer interval than the district hotspots, but any map-based conclusion about northern extent is unreliable until the coordinate is confirmed.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for a mid-color isolated dot far to the north of the dense Gandhinagar-Kalol cluster — the color shows moderate salinity, the position is the warning.

insights.title: Confined-aquifer TDS of 710 mg/L in May 2017
insights.explanation: A tube well in the confined User Aquifer at Unava recorded 710 mg/L TDS in the May 2017 premonsoon round. It is part of the GWRDC Ltd. confined-aquifer quality network mapped as TDS of the User Aquifer for premonsoon 2017.

insights.title: Mid-range for the Gandhinagar confined network
insights.explanation: Unava sits in the middle of the district range: similar to Gandhinagar-II at 800 mg/L and Limbodara at 830 mg/L, above Bhat-II at 410 mg/L and Dingucha-II at 430 mg/L, and well below saline hotspots like Dingucha-I at 1590 mg/L and Nasmed at 3210 mg/L. It signals moderate mineralization, not freshest nor most saline in this confined system.

insights.title: Northern outlier location to verify
insights.explanation: Unava is listed at 24.3675°N with an explicit lat-outlier-verify flag, while peer confined stations cluster around 23.10°N to 23.38°N at similar longitude. On a map it will appear as an isolated northern dot well outside the main Gandhinagar-Kalol cloud, so verify coordinates before using it for spacing, interpolation, or site selection.

narrative.secondary_context: Listed longitude ~72.66°E is consistent with the district cluster; only latitude is anomalous. TDS value itself is usable as a point record even while position is checked.

narrative.headline: Mid-range deep salinity in Gandhinagar city amid sharp district contrasts
narrative.summary: Gandhinagar-I recorded 770 mg/L TDS in its May 2017 confined sample, very close to neighboring Gandhinagar-II at 800 mg/L. That places the city site in a middle, more usable band while western parts of the district reach 1,500 to over 3,200 mg/L. The contrast highlights locally variable deep quality rather than a uniform aquifer.
narrative.why_it_matters: For planning, the mid-range city value suggests lower mineral load and treatment burden than the western saline zones, but the sharp nearby variation means any expansion cannot assume the same quality a few kilometres away.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for a mid-tone marker at Gandhinagar city — darker than the fresher Bhat pocket to the south, but much lighter than the high-salinity hotspots to the west.

insights.title: City-center confined water is moderately mineralized
insights.explanation: The station's confined sample was 770 mg/L TDS in pre-monsoon May 2017. It closely matches nearby Gandhinagar-II at 800 mg/L, indicating a consistent mid-range city-center zone within the monitored User Aquifer network mapped in Fig.18.

insights.title: Same aquifer varies from fresh to highly saline nearby
insights.explanation: Bhat-II to the south is fresher at 410 mg/L, while values rise sharply outward to 1,300 mg/L at Pundhra-I, 1,590 mg/L at Dingucha-I and 3,210 mg/L at Nasmed. This shows salinity in the same confined system can more than quadruple within the district, making Gandhinagar-I relatively favorable but not uniformly representative.

insights.title: Part of a district-wide confined-aquifer quality snapshot
insights.explanation: The value comes from the systematic tube-well quality monitoring used for the 2017 pre-monsoon TDS map. Even adjacent sites like Dingucha-I and Dingucha-II differ greatly at 1,590 versus 430 mg/L, and Limbodara sits at 830 mg/L, so local screening and continued monitoring matter more than district averages.

narrative.secondary_context: Confined User Aquifer in Gandhinagar district, Gujarat — pre-monsoon May 2017 tube-well survey.

narrative.headline: Koba shows fresher confined water in a patchy salinity landscape
narrative.summary: The confined aquifer at Koba recorded 520 mg/L TDS in May 2017, placing it toward the fresher side of local results. Nearby stations range from about 410 mg/L to over 3,000 mg/L, so Koba stands out as relatively low-salinity for that snapshot.
narrative.why_it_matters: Salinity patchiness controls where deeper groundwater is easier to use and manage. Koba's mid-low value suggests more favorable quality at this spot in 2017, while the nearby highs flag heterogeneity and risk that needs local screening.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Find Koba south of the Gandhinagar cluster as a lower-value point, and contrast it with the much higher dots to the west at Nasmed and north at Dingucha-I.

insights.title: Moderate TDS at Koba in May 2017
insights.explanation: A tube-well sample from the confined aquifer at Koba recorded 520 mg/L TDS in the May 2017 pre-monsoon round. This is a single-point measured snapshot of the deeper User Aquifer, not a trend.

insights.title: Lower-mid range versus neighbours
insights.explanation: Koba at 520 mg/L sits close to the fresher end seen at Bhat-II at 410 mg/L and Dingucha-II at 430 mg/L, and below nearby Gandhinagar-II at 800 mg/L and Limbodara at 830 mg/L. It is sharply lower than high-salinity records at Dingucha-I at 1,590 mg/L and Nasmed at 3,210 mg/L, highlighting strong local variability within the same confined monitoring set.

insights.title: Part of regional confined-aquifer mapping
insights.explanation: Koba is one point in a GWRDC programme monitoring tube-well quality, compiled as a pre-monsoon 2017 TDS map of the User Aquifer. That regional view is the right context for judging whether Koba is a local fresher pocket or part of a broader pattern.

features.location_description: Bhat-I, Gandhinagar taluka; same coords as Bhat-II
features.name: Bhat-I

narrative.headline: Bhat-I shows moderate salinity — but its twin well at the same site is much fresher
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the confined aquifer at Bhat-I measured 750 mg/L total dissolved solids. A second record at the identical coordinates, Bhat-II, measured only 410 mg/L, highlighting sharp within-site variation in the user aquifer monitored across Gandhinagar.
narrative.why_it_matters: Water quality here cannot be assumed from location alone — depth or screened interval likely drives the difference, so any future supply or treatment planning at this site needs well-specific testing rather than relying on a neighborhood average.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Zoom to Bhat in Gandhinagar taluka and look for two overlapping confined-aquifer points — the higher-value Bhat-I sits directly on the much fresher Bhat-II.

insights.title: 750 mg/L confined TDS at Bhat-I
insights.explanation: Pre-monsoon May 2017 sampling of the confined aquifer at Bhat-I in Gandhinagar taluka recorded 750 mg/L total dissolved solids.

insights.title: Same coordinates, very different water
insights.explanation: Bhat-II at the identical coordinates recorded only 410 mg/L, almost half the Bhat-I value. The same paired-well pattern appears at Dingucha, where Dingucha-I recorded 1590 mg/L and Dingucha-II only 430 mg/L, indicating sharp vertical or screen-interval variation rather than mapping error.

insights.title: Part of district-wide pre-monsoon quality mapping
insights.explanation: These wells are part of GWRDC monitoring of tube wells used to map TDS of the User Aquifer in pre-monsoon 2017. Nearby Gandhinagar-II at 800 mg/L and Limbodara at 830 mg/L are close to Bhat-I, while Nasmed at 3210 mg/L shows the district high end, placing Bhat-I in the middle of a highly variable confined system.

narrative.secondary_context: Pre-monsoon May 2017 GWRDC survey of confined (User) aquifer TDS across Gandhinagar district.

narrative.headline: A saltier pocket in the deep aquifer at AdrajMoti
narrative.summary: Deep confined groundwater at AdrajMoti measured 1,160 mg/L TDS in May 2017 pre-monsoon sampling. That is saltier than fresher stations nearby at 410-830 mg/L, but below the most saline pockets above 1,300 mg/L elsewhere in the district. The pattern points to patchy salinity in the used deep aquifer.
narrative.why_it_matters: For anyone relying on the deep aquifer here, this signals more mineralized water that may need more attention to treatment, blending, or well siting than fresher zones, and nearby wells cannot be assumed to have the same quality.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for AdrajMoti as a mid-high color on the confined-aquifer TDS map — darker than the fresher spots to the south, lighter than the extreme highs to the west and north.

insights.title: Pre-monsoon deep-aquifer salinity reading
insights.explanation: This station is part of GWRDC Ltd. tube-well monitoring of the used confined aquifer, mapped as pre-monsoon 2017 TDS in Fig.18. The May 2017 confined sample here measured 1160 mg/L TDS, indicating distinctly mineralized deep groundwater at this location.

insights.title: Above fresher neighbours, below saline extremes
insights.explanation: At 1160 mg/L, AdrajMoti sits above fresher confined readings nearby such as Bhat-II at 410 mg/L, Gandhinagar-II at 800 mg/L and Limbodara at 830 mg/L. It sits below the more saline confined readings at Dingucha-I at 1590 mg/L, Pundhra-I at 1300 mg/L and Nasmed at 3210 mg/L, placing it in the upper-middle of the district range.

insights.title: Patchy salinity over short distances
insights.explanation: Salinity changes sharply over very short distances in this aquifer: Dingucha-I recorded 1590 mg/L and Dingucha-II recorded 430 mg/L at essentially the same coordinates. That patchiness means AdrajMoti's 1160 mg/L reflects a local pocket rather than a uniform district trend.

narrative.secondary_context: Pre-monsoon May 2017 survey of the used confined aquifer across Gandhinagar district.

narrative.headline: Moderate salinity at IsanpurMota-II sits between two very different neighbours at the same site
narrative.summary: Confined groundwater at IsanpurMota-II measured 570 mg/L TDS in May 2017. At essentially the same location, companion wells recorded 440 and 820 mg/L, while the wider Gandhinagar confined network ranged from about 410 to over 1,100 mg/L.
narrative.why_it_matters: The spread at a single village shows quality can change sharply over very short distance or depth, so one well cannot stand in for the whole site. This middle value indicates moderate mineral load, but the nearby 820 mg/L result means design should allow for zone-specific testing and treatment flexibility.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Zoom to the IsanpurMota cluster: three tightly grouped points stepping from lower to middle to higher TDS, paler than the high-value points farther north around Mansa.

insights.title: Confined TDS of 570 mg/L in May 2017
insights.explanation: Direct May-2017 record for the confined aquifer at IsanpurMota-II is 570 mg/L TDS, establishing the anchor value for this station.

insights.title: Sharp local contrast at the same village
insights.explanation: At essentially the same coordinates, IsanpurMota-I measured 440 mg/L and IsanpurMota-III measured 820 mg/L, so IsanpurMota-II sits in the middle of a ~380 mg/L spread within one village footprint.

insights.title: Mid-range in a district-wide gradient
insights.explanation: In the wider Gandhinagar confined network, lower values occur to the south and west at Bhat-II at 410 mg/L and Dingucha-II at 430 mg/L, while higher values occur nearby at Gandhinagar-II at 800 mg/L and farther north at Rangpur-II at 990 mg/L and Pundhra-II at 1140 mg/L, placing IsanpurMota-II in the moderate middle of a south-to-north increase.

narrative.secondary_context: May 2017 confined-aquifer TDS snapshot for Gandhinagar district; IsanpurMota I, II and III are co-located records that allow local comparison.

narrative.headline: Saltiest well in its own cluster in a protected, falling deep aquifer
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the confined aquifer at IsanpurMota-III recorded 820 mg/L TDS, nearly double the co-located IsanpurMota-I value of 440 mg/L. The same station shows a falling 2008-2017 level trend in Confined Aquifer Group-II within a deep interval where tapping in Gandhinagar taluka is limited to drinking and domestic use.
narrative.why_it_matters: For planning, this is not just more mineralized water but mineralized water in a declining, regulated deep system, so future supply depends on managing existing wells and understanding local variation rather than assuming uniform quality.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for a high-value dot overlapping two much lower-value dots at Isanpur Mota — the color jump marks the salinity pocket — then check the deep-aquifer trend and protected-zone overlay.

insights.title: Elevated confined-aquifer salinity at this station
insights.explanation: GWRDC tube-well monitoring recorded 820 mg/L TDS in the confined aquifer here in May 2017 pre-monsoon, the value mapped as part of the User Aquifer TDS survey.

insights.title: Stark contrast within the same site cluster
insights.explanation: Two wells at essentially the same location recorded much fresher water at the same time — 440 mg/L at IsanpurMota-I and 570 mg/L at IsanpurMota-II — versus 820 mg/L at IsanpurMota-III, showing sharp variation over very short distance or depth.

insights.title: High end of the district picture
insights.explanation: Regionally the 820 mg/L value sits at the high end compared with other May 2017 confined results such as 660 mg/L at Kharna-III in Mansa and 400 mg/L at Dehgam-III, underscoring that this is a locally mineralized pocket rather than uniform background.

insights.title: Falling long-term water level
insights.explanation: For 2008-2017 the station's Confined Aquifer Group-II record shows a falling trend of -1.10152, meaning higher salinity coincides with a long-term declining head.

insights.title: Deep zone carries use restrictions
insights.explanation: Confined Aquifer-III at 200-300 m overlaps the protected interval below 200 m in Gandhinagar Taluka, where tapping is restricted to drinking and domestic use, which limits options to simply drill deeper for fresher supply.

narrative.headline: Aluva shows fresher confined water amid saltier Kalol wells
narrative.summary: Aluva's confined aquifer measured 420 mg/L TDS in May 2017, among the freshest values in the Kalol set. Nearby confined wells ranged up to 3,210 mg/L, highlighting highly variable water quality over short distances.
narrative.why_it_matters: Fresher pockets like Aluva are more attractive for sustained use because they imply lower salinity load, while the surrounding variability signals risk in assuming uniform quality across Kalol for planning.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Aluva as a low-value point surrounded by higher-value neighbours in the confined TDS layer — a local fresher pocket within a saltier zone.

insights.title: Low-salinity confined measurement at Aluva
insights.explanation: The station at Aluva in Kalol taluka recorded 420 mg/L TDS in the confined aquifer in pre-monsoon May 2017, representing a relatively fresh confined-water measurement for this area.

insights.title: Sharp local contrast across Kalol
insights.explanation: Other Kalol confined wells in the same May 2017 round were substantially saltier: 1,590 mg/L at Dingucha-I, 830 mg/L at Limbodara, 960 mg/L at Bhoyan Moti, 740 mg/L at Rancharada, and 3,210 mg/L at Nasmed. Even co-located Dingucha-II at 430 mg/L versus Dingucha-I at 1,590 mg/L shows sharp local variation, making Aluva's 420 mg/L one of the freshest points in a patchy field.

insights.title: Part of systematic confined-aquifer mapping
insights.explanation: This value comes from the GWRDC tube-well monitoring programme for the User Aquifer, compiled as a pre-monsoon 2017 TDS map. Aluva should therefore be read as one monitored point in a regional quality pattern, not an isolated sample.

narrative.secondary_context: Longitude for Aluva is truncated with low coordinate precision, so treat its plotted position as approximate when comparing to neighbouring wells.

narrative.headline: Fresher confined-water pocket at Kharna in a variable Mansa belt
narrative.summary: Kharna-I recorded 780 mg/L TDS in the confined aquifer in May 2017, part of a fresher Kharna-Rangpur pocket. Values rise sharply eastward to over 1100-1300 mg/L at Pundhra. A 2008-2017 falling trend at nearby Kharna-III shows quality strength coexists with quantity stress.
narrative.why_it_matters: For siting wells or planning supply, Kharna offers lower-salinity confined water than much of surrounding Mansa, but the nearby declining level trend means reliability depends on managing pumping, not quality alone.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for the lower-value Kharna cluster against higher, darker TDS points to the east around Pundhra — a local fresher zone within a patchy salinity map.

insights.title: Moderate salinity measured in confined aquifer
insights.explanation: A pre-monsoon May 2017 sample from the confined aquifer at Kharna-I measured 780 mg/L total dissolved solids. It comes from the GWRDC tube-well quality monitoring network used to map user-aquifer TDS across the area.

insights.title: Kharna stands out as fresher than eastern stations
insights.explanation: Kharna-I at 780 mg/L sits with its almost-co-located neighbour Kharna-III at 660 mg/L and Rangpur-I at 740 mg/L, well below Pundhra-I at 1300 mg/L and Pundhra-II at 1140 mg/L to the east, and below Rangpur-II at 990 mg/L. That makes Kharna one of the fresher points in this Mansa taluka cluster for May 2017.

insights.title: Nearby long-term fall signal tempers the good-quality picture
insights.explanation: At nearby Kharna-III, the 2008-2017 record for Confined Aquifer Group-II shows a falling trend value of -0.75636. Quality here looks relatively favourable, but the quantity signal suggests the deeper resource has been under pressure.

narrative.secondary_context: Premonsoon May 2017 confined-aquifer TDS survey in Mansa taluka, Gandhinagar district.

narrative.headline: Kharna-III is a fresher-water pocket in Mansa, but its deep aquifer is trending down
narrative.summary: Kharna-III recorded 660 mg/L TDS in the confined aquifer in May 2017, making it one of the fresher points in Mansa compared to Kharna-I and the much saltier Pundhra stations. The same station's Confined Aquifer Group-II shows a falling trend over 2008-2017, so better quality coincides with sustained pressure on deep water levels.
narrative.why_it_matters: For planning, Kharna-III points to a relatively better-quality confined source within a variable taluka already rated suitable for drinking and irrigation, but the falling deep-aquifer trend means future use depends on managing levels, not just quality.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Kharna-III in western Mansa as a lower-value point versus higher values to the east at Pundhra; overlay the 2008-2017 trend to see the falling signal in the deep confined zone beneath this fresher quality.

insights.title: Relatively fresh confined water measured at Kharna-III
insights.explanation: Kharna-III in Mansa taluka recorded 660 mg/L TDS in the confined aquifer in May 2017. It comes from the GWRDC tube-well quality monitoring used to map pre-monsoon 2017 TDS of the used confined aquifer.

insights.title: Fresher than nearby Mansa stations
insights.explanation: At 660 mg/L, Kharna-III is fresher than its almost co-located neighbor Kharna-I at 780 mg/L and markedly fresher than Pundhra-I at 1300 mg/L and Pundhra-II at 1140 mg/L in the same taluka, highlighting strong local variability within Mansa's confined system.

insights.title: Decade-long falling trend in the deep aquifer
insights.explanation: For Confined Aquifer Group-II at Kharna-III, the reported 2008-2017 trend value is -0.75636 with a Fall direction. Quality advantage therefore coexists with a decade-long declining water-level signal in the deep system.

insights.title: Stacked Mansa aquifers provide the context
insights.explanation: Mansa has a stacked system: phreatic 0 to 70 m, Confined I 100 to 150 m, Confined II 185 to 210 m, and Confined III 260 to 300 m, with the summary table marking suitability for drinking and irrigation as Yes. Kharna is one of several villages monitored with repeat -I/-II/-III stations, and Mansa has 6 stations in the district network.

narrative.secondary_context: Part of a 30-station confined-aquifer TDS survey across Gandhinagar, Kalol, Mansa and Dehgam; peer Mansa confined values in the dataset range up to 1300 mg/L, placing Kharna-III at the low end.

narrative.headline: Rangpur-I shows fresher confined water in eastern Mansa
narrative.summary: Pre-monsoon 2017 monitoring recorded 740 mg/L TDS in the confined aquifer at Rangpur-I, Mansa taluka. That is lower than adjacent Rangpur-II and the Pundhra wells and sits at the fresher, eastern end of a regional gradient that increases westward.
narrative.why_it_matters: This eastern pocket indicates lower salinity pressure in the deep aquifer compared with sites to the west, which matters for where to prioritize deeper supply and where to watch for rising salinity and treatment needs.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In the TDS map view, look for the eastern Mansa cluster — Rangpur-I shows as a lower-value point among nearby higher readings, before values darken westward toward higher salinity.

insights.title: 740 mg/L confined TDS in May 2017
insights.explanation: Pre-monsoon 2017 monitoring of the confined tube-well network recorded 740 mg/L TDS at Rangpur-I. It is a direct observation of the deep user aquifer, part of the systematic quality monitoring mapped for 2017.

insights.title: Fresher than nearby wells
insights.explanation: Rangpur-I at 740 mg/L is fresher than its immediate neighbour Rangpur-II at 990 mg/L and distinctly fresher than Pundhra-I at 1300 mg/L and Pundhra-II at 1140 mg/L to the northwest. It aligns more closely with Kharna-I at 780 mg/L and Kharna-III at 660 mg/L, marking it as part of a lower-salinity pocket within this Mansa cluster.

insights.title: Fits regional east-to-west pattern
insights.explanation: The source interprets confined-aquifer quality as deteriorating from east to west in the flow direction, with TDS ranging from about 500 mg/L to over 2700 mg/L and the major part below 2000 mg/L, with higher values in the west around Chhatral. Rangpur-I in eastern Mansa sits on the fresher, eastern side of that gradient.

narrative.headline: Rangpur-II shows mid-range salinity in Mansa's patchy deep aquifer
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the confined well at Rangpur-II recorded 990 mg/L dissolved solids. It falls between fresher water at Rangpur-I and saltier water at Pundhra-II, highlighting sharp local variability in Mansa's widely used confined system.
narrative.why_it_matters: For siting and supply planning, this shows deep groundwater here is productive and actively tracked, but quality cannot be extrapolated from one village to the next — site-specific testing and allowance for treatment or blending drive usability and cost.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Locate Rangpur-II in Mansa taluka and compare its pre-monsoon 2017 TDS marker to Rangpur-I immediately alongside it and Pundhra-II to the northwest — a clear step-up in salinity over a short distance at about 100-120 m depth.

insights.title: 990 mg/L confined reading in May 2017
insights.explanation: Pre-monsoon May 2017 sampling recorded 990 mg/L TDS in the confined aquifer at Rangpur-II, as part of the tube-well quality monitoring and TDS mapping of the user aquifer.

insights.title: Fresher next door, saltier nearby
insights.explanation: Rangpur-II at 990 mg/L sits well above nearby Rangpur-I at 740 mg/L but below Pundhra-II at 1140 mg/L, showing salinity changes of hundreds of mg/L over short distances in Mansa.

insights.title: Deep, stacked aquifer in dual use
