Kalol's piezometer to about 202.5 m is logged much more finely to the centimetre and shows the same rhythm at smaller scale, including fine sand with silt, sand with gravel/kankar and clay-mixed sand. Palaz and Pethapur both stop at 202 m with yellowish subrounded sands that coarsen downward interbedded with soapy yellow clays and 14-17-m mixed zones, and Sardhav extends the same brown/reddish-brown sand-versus-clay motif to about 344 m, with its longest clay plugs 34 m thick at 112-146 m and 25 m at 263-288 m. In practical terms, the sands and gravelly sands are the water carriers, the thick sticky clays are the seals that make water below them pressurized, and the many thin mixed zones are leaky transitions. That is why a tube-well has to be 120 m or deeper to be reliable here, while a dug-well only sees the top unconfined fringe.

District-wide pictures of groundwater only mean something if they are anchored in what was actually seen in the ground. In Gandhinagar this anchor is a small set of deep, layer-by-layer borehole descriptions — lithologs — from Sertha, Kalol, Palaz, Pethapur and Sardhav. Together they let us zoom from taluka and block averages down to metres of sand, silt, clay, kanker and gravel. All five tell a similar first story: a thin topsoil, then an alternation of yellowish-brown sands and sticky brown to yellowish clays, with coarser gravelly or kankar-bearing sands marking the more permeable zones. The differences are in depth and detail. Sertha is the only hole that goes beyond 300 m, to 353 m, and bottoms in dark clay and claystone — the deepest control for any cross-section. Kalol stops at about 202.5 m but is logged in fine detail, even to centimetres, and shows characteristic shallow sands over deeper fine-to-coarse sands with gravel. Palaz and Pethapur both stop at about 202 m and show the same rhythmic 2 to 18 m sand-clay cycles, and Sardhav reaches to about 300 m plus a deeper 324-344 m snippet. Read together, they confirm a stacked alluvial system of repeated sand bodies separated by clays, not one continuous sand sheet. Equally important is what they do not contain: no coordinates, dates, water strikes, screens or pumping-test data in the supplied tables, plus overlaps, a 24-m gap at Sardhav, and a long verbatim duplication between Palaz and Pethapur. That means local profiles are strong on rock type and layer order, but weak as stand-alone proof of water levels, yields or lateral continuity without cleaning and correlation to the monitoring network.

Gandhinagar District looks flat and fairly uniform from the road, but the ground underneath is not one big underground tank. It is a layered cake of sands that can hold and give water, separated by clays that mostly block it. The district synthesis describes a shallow, unconfined phreatic aquifer near the surface plus three deeper confined aquifers, and the direct drilling logs show why that layering matters street by street. In Khadat in Gandhinagar Taluka, for example, the top 60 metres are mostly brown and yellowish sands and silts you could pump from, then the hole turns almost entirely blue-grey clay and sandy clay down to 198 m. A few kilometres away at Chiloda the same shallow zone is yellowish silty sand with hard Kankar nodules and a distinctive pink feldspar-plus-quartz sand at 30-42 m, then interbedded clay and sandy clay to 201 m. That local switching between sand and clay over tens of metres is the rule, not the exception. Deeper drilling at Giyod proves the pattern continues downward. After 52 m of fine surface material there is a 64-m-thick package of fine-to-coarse sand with quartzite plus clay lenses from 52-116 m — a very good target — followed by mixed sands and clays, and then three very thick sticky grey clays: 118 m thick from 188-306 m, 79 m from 327-406 m, and about 45 m at the bottom to 450.94 m. Those thick clays are what make the deep aquifers confined and protected, but they also mean you cannot expect the same depth to work everywhere. At the other end of the scale, Gram Bharti (Amrapur) shows a shallow, clean, well-sorted sand from 0-40 m, a thin 5-m gravel with quartz, feldspar and black fragments at 40-45 m, and then a soapy, slippery clay from 45-58 m where the record stops. It is a promising shallow zone with only a thin cap, so it is both productive and vulnerable to pollution and drying. The logs also warn us not to over-interpret. Two boreholes, Palaz and Pethapur, repeat near-identical wording for 61-202 m, which looks like copy-paste rather than two independent observations. Chhalla’s table has garbled depth figures that still resolve to about 200.75 m total with topsoil 0-7 m, pinkish-yellow sands, brown and dark-grey gravels, and grey sands down to about 182 m capped by dark bluish-grey basal clay. Gram Bharti is truncated at 58 m. In short: sands give the water, clays decide where it stays, thickness changes quickly, and good local decisions need careful, well-by-well checking.

Zooming in changes the story. At district scale Gandhinagar looks like layer upon layer of sand and clay, but the actual wells show that each taluka — and even neighbouring villages — has a different underground architecture. This chapter stays close to what drillers actually saw, metre by metre. In Dahegam in the east, two deep boreholes both hit hard basalt basement, but not at the same depth, and both are sealed by more than 140 metres of sticky grey-to-blue clay. That thick clay is the lid that separates shallow, easy-to-reach water from deeper confined water. In Gandhinagar taluka itself, the picture is almost the opposite: at Giyod the drill went to about 451 m and never hit basement at all, passing instead through alternating sands and two very thick clay blocks more than 70–118 m thick. Near the surface, however, the same taluka is remarkably consistent: a well-sorted yellowish-brown sand in the top 30–40 m, often with a thin gravel or kankar band, then a first clay at 40–60 m. That top triplet is the unconfined aquifer most open wells tap. At Ranasan, the drill finally shows what happens when the alluvium ends: fractured, weathered and vesicular basalt with zeolite and calcite fillings from about 227.5 m down to 337.6 m, a type of hard rock that can still carry water in its cracks. Farther north in Mansa, the Itadra borehole went to 452 m — the deepest in this set — without hitting any basement, alternating between brown sand-with-gravel, sandy clay with kankar, and a massive 80-m reddish-brown sandy clay at 291–370 m. Together these direct logs explain why water levels, quality and drilling success change over short distances: thickness of the clay lid, depth to basement, and whether the sand is clean quartzite sand or mixed sand-and-clay decides where water sits and how well it is protected.

Zooming out to the whole district hides how different one taluka looks from the next once you put a drill rig on the ground. This chapter stays close to the wells themselves: the block-level summaries for places like Mansa and Kalol, the deep exploratory and piezometer holes that prove what is down there, the small inventory wells that farmers actually use, and the foot-by-foot descriptions of sand, sandy clay, clay and finally hard rock.

The big picture from the holes is a layered cake, not one big underground tank. A shallow, unconfined sandy zone that you can dig or bore into directly is followed downward by thick clays that seal off deeper, pressurized sands. In Mansa that shallow zone is described to about 70 m, then three confined aquifers at roughly 100-150 m, 185-210 m and 260-300 m. Kalol looks very similar but its shallow zone is described as thicker, to about 90 m, with its three confined sands at about 110-150 m, 165-190 m and 240-300 m. The district synthesis uses slightly wider ranges for the same three confined systems, which is expected because depth to a sand shifts from village to village.

The cuttings themselves explain why drillers and scientists talk about lenses and intercalations rather than clean sheets of sand. At Ranasan the top is fine quartz sand, then a more than 20-m thick mostly-sandy mixed zone with silt lenses, then repeated brown medium to coarse sands separated by yellowish clays and silty-clay mixes. At Nardipur the top 130 m is an even busier alternation: 2- to 26-m thick slices of silty sand, fine sand, clayey sand, sticky brown clay and a quartz-rich sand-plus-gravel at 95-121 m. At Moti Bardoli a single clay aquitard is logged from 82 to 235 m, more than 150 m thick, which is why the aquifers above and below it behave independently. Sertha, Khadat, Chiloda, Pore-Gandhinagar, Grambharti and Kalol piezometers all repeat the same language: brown to yellowish fine to medium sand, sometimes with gravel or kankar, grading into sandy clay and sticky clay.

The bottom of the story is hard rock. Several deep logs pass out of alluvium into reddish-brown to grey basalt, sometimes vesicular or amygdaloidal with zeolite/calcite, sometimes weathered and fractured, and in one hole into quartzite, sandstone and grey claystone before basalt. That basement is the floor: there is no deeper alluvial water to chase below it. Spot chemistry from the same well network shows why local checks matter. A Bhat-II confined sample is fresh near 410 mg/L TDS while not far away Kadjodra unconfined water is about 1,320 mg/L, Dingucha-I is about 1,590 mg/L and Nasmed reaches about 3,210 mg/L. Fresh pockets and brackish pockets sit side by side, so a district average cannot tell a village what its well will taste like.

District averages hide what a driller actually meets. In Dahegam in the east, you can hit hard basalt rock at about 227-268 m depth after drilling through more than 140 m of sticky grey-blue clay, while a few kilometres away at Itadra in Mansa or at Nardipur you can drill to 300-450 m and still be in sand and clay with no rock at all. The logs show why: a shallow soil-and-clay blanket 0-50 m thick, then a very promising gravel-and-sand zone from about 51-139 m at Dahegam, then a return to clay that can be 60 m thick locally and 140-190 m thick regionally. That thick clay is the seal that separates shallow, unconfined water that rises and falls with rain from deeper, confined water that is under pressure. Village-scale logs at Kasturinagar-IFFCO (only 44 m deep) and Sanoda-Gandhinagar (99 m deep) make the same point at small scale: water lives not in one big underground lake but in thin 3-15 m lenses of sand, kankar and gravel sandwiched between clays. Reading those depth-by-depth sequences together with where basement was or was not met explains why well depths, yields and feasibility change from taluka to taluka and even village to village.

District and taluka maps tell you where water should be. The drilled wells tell you what is actually there. In this area the direct evidence comes mainly from three detailed logs: a 202.5-m piezometer at Kalol, a very deep 450-m borehole at Pore-Gandhinagar, and a shallow 3-99 m sequence at Sanoda-Gandhinagar plus a 99-200.5 m tail whose village name was lost in the table extraction. Read top to bottom, all three show the same alluvial style - sand, silt, kankar and gravel alternating with sticky clay - but the thickness, colour and continuity of the sands change with depth. Those changes are what allow hydrogeologists to separate a thin unconfined cover from deeper confined aquifers, and to flag where good aquifer sands are thick enough to tap.

findings.title: Living beyond the renewable limit
findings.statement: All four assessment units and the district as a whole are Over-Exploited: withdrawals exceed the portion that can be renewed each year, leaving zero for future use.
findings.why_it_matters: When use is 104–139% of renewable supply, water levels keep falling, shallow wells go dry, quality worsens, and any new demand must come from saving, recharge or outside sources like the Narmada canal — not from more pumping.
findings.scope: Gandhinagar District and Dehgam, Gandhinagar, Kalol, Mansa talukas

findings.title: How supply and the safe limit were calculated
findings.statement: Resources were estimated jointly with the Gujarat government using GEC-15 norms after district reorganisation: total recharge minus 5% natural discharge equals the extractable amount, ranging from 9,074 Ham in Mansa to 14,660 Ham in Dehgam.
findings.why_it_matters: A common, dated method lets villages, talukas and the state compare fairly and shows why even the wettest taluka cannot meet its pumping — the safe limit is gross recharge minus nature's share, not the full rainfall.

findings.title: Farming drives the deficit
findings.statement: Irrigation accounts for about 96% of pumping district-wide, so even modest farm savings matter most; towns also need reserved drinking water for 2025, tightening the squeeze, with Kalol at 114% and Gandhinagar at 104% also over the limit.
findings.why_it_matters: Because almost every extra bucket comes from fields, measures like efficient irrigation, crop choices and metering farm power do more for future drinking water and food security than small domestic cuts alone.

findings.title: A deep reserve with little room for error
findings.statement: The deepest productive zone lies 200–300 m down with very deep static levels and no long-term level history; it is being tapped but needs testing, while law already restricts wells below 200 m in Gandhinagar Taluka to drinking use and notifies Kalol for controlled abstraction.
findings.why_it_matters: Deep water is costly, slow to refill and, once depleted or contaminated, hard to restore — protection and careful exploration prevent a short-term fix from becoming a permanent loss for drinking-water security.
findings.scope: Confined Aquifer Group-III 200-300 m, Gandhinagar and Kalol talukas

findings.title: Plenty of space, no spare water
findings.statement: There is huge empty space underground that could theoretically store over 2,000 MCM, but only about 12 MCM per year of spare runoff exists and existing structures already use more than that, so no additional large check dams or percolation tanks are recommended.
findings.why_it_matters: It reframes hope: building more of the same large structures without water to fill them wastes money — success now depends on rooftop harvesting, recharge wells, pond desilting and saving water rather than capturing new runoff.
findings.pattern_type: large storage potential versus no surplus water

findings.title: What care looks like on the ground
findings.statement: The plan calls for four tracks together — supply-side recharge, demand-side savings, regulation and institutions — already shown in pilots like IFFCO's trench-plus-wells at Sertha, a converted failed well at Tara na Chhapra recharging about 20 litres per second, and soft-rock percolation tanks and recharge shafts suited to Dahegam.
findings.why_it_matters: Because no single fix works where water is uneven and overused, small, local successes that turn failed wells and village ponds into recharge points, plus enforced rules, give communities a practical path to slow declines and protect drinking supplies.

findings.title: Every taluka starts over-exploited
findings.statement: All four talukas were Over-Exploited in 2017: Dahegam 106.31%, Gandhinagar 104.02%, Kalol 114.08% and Mansa 139.35%. Mansa stands out as the most stressed, with withdrawals more than one-third above the sustainable limit.
findings.why_it_matters: Starting from over-exploitation everywhere means there is no surplus taluka to compensate for others; management must reduce use district-wide, with the greatest urgency in Mansa.
findings.scope: Dahegam, Gandhinagar, Kalol, Mansa talukas; Gandhinagar District baseline 2017

findings.title: How recharge and usable water were estimated
findings.statement: Recharge and extractable volumes were derived by converting feasible area to rock volume with a 6-m / 3-m thickness rule and then to water with a specific yield of 0.15 (for example Dehgam-area x 0.15). After that accounting, only 12.17 MCM of surplus runoff remained, while existing structures already account for 41.55 MCM, leaving a Nil balance for new work.
findings.why_it_matters: The method makes clear why supply cannot solve the gap: the arithmetic leaves almost no unused runoff, so expectations for new recharge construction must be reset toward maintaining existing capacity.

findings.title: Saving water by using less
findings.statement: About 81,782 ha are irrigated with groundwater and only 15,030 ha (~19%) are already under micro-irrigation. The plan proposes 46,726 ha more (70% of the remainder, added at ~15% of balance area per year) using Draft-for-MIS = Area x Delta x 0.3 /10, cutting irrigation draft from 511.14 MCM to 441.05 MCM for a saving of 70.09 MCM. Dahegam, Gandhinagar, Kalol and Mansa contribute proposed areas of 9,932 ha, 11,392 ha, 12,944 ha and 12,459 ha respectively.
findings.why_it_matters: Efficiency is the largest available lever: the same cropped area can be sustained with about 70 MCM less pumping, directly lowering the over-exploitation stages without depending on uncertain extra runoff.
findings.scope: District and taluka irrigation draft and micro-irrigation areas

findings.title: No room for new supply structures
findings.statement: Artificial recharge is not proposed because recharge capacity through existing structures exceeds the surplus non-committed runoff, and no check dams or percolation tanks are suggested as non-committed runoff is not available. Existing structures are expected to recharge all of the surplus, and feasible recharge areas shown for reference require no new construction.
findings.why_it_matters: It prevents wasteful investment in structures with no water to capture, and shifts attention and funds to maintaining existing check dams/tanks and to demand measures.
findings.scope: District supply-side and artificial recharge feasibility

findings.title: What the future could look like — and its limits
findings.statement: With phased micro-irrigation the district could be brought to ~97.29% and kept within 100% in the long run, with Dahegam (98.46%), Gandhinagar (93.79%) and Kalol (99.63%) improving to Critical while Mansa (122.31%) stays Over-Exploited. The deepest reserve framing this future is Confined Aquifer Group-III at about 200-300 m (Kalol 240-300 m; Mansa 260-300 m). Drip spread is held back because many wells are shared on partnership and partners do not agree to share a well for drip, despite subsidies and farmer interest.
findings.why_it_matters: Even full delivery of the efficiency plan does not heal Mansa, and continued pressure would fall on the deep 200-300 m zone; lasting care needs targeted action in Mansa and solutions to shared-well barriers, plus protection of the deepest aquifer.
findings.scope: Taluka categories after intervention; deepest confined aquifer Group-III 200-300 m

findings.title: Most shallow and deeper water is fresh by the official saltiness test
findings.statement: Groundwater in the district is described as in general potable and fresh in both phreatic (shallow) and confined (deeper) aquifers within 200 m, with shallow-aquifer TDS everywhere within the permissible limit and most confined water also below it.
findings.why_it_matters: Tells a non-technical reader that, as a rule, well water can be used for drinking, but the word 'most' leaves room for local exceptions that need checking against the 500 desirable and 2000 permissible limits.
findings.scope: Gandhinagar District, phreatic and confined aquifers within ~200 m depth

findings.title: What the shallow-water laboratory snapshot looked like in May 2017
findings.statement: The detailed May 2017 shallow-water table shows a narrow, moderately salty snapshot: TDS 1072 (Gandhinagar) to 1090 (Dahegam), conductance 1600-1627 uS/cm, bicarbonate 317-659, chloride 149-213, nitrate 95-125, sulphate 2-91, calcium 12-96, magnesium 46-125, sodium ~188-190, potassium 0.4-21.0, iron 0.16-1.90, and fluoride 1.25-2.65 mg/l.
findings.why_it_matters: Shows that even when saltiness is acceptable, other things like hardness and fluoride can affect taste, health and treatment needs; the fluoride top value already exceeds the drinking limit.
findings.scope: Unconfined aquifer, May 2017 monitoring stations summarized as Gandhinagar vs Dahegam minima/maxima

findings.title: Deeper water gets saltier toward the west
findings.statement: Confined groundwater quality deteriorates from east to western parts in the groundwater flow direction, with TDS varying from about 500 mg/l to more than 2700 mg/l and higher values in the west around Chhatral.
findings.why_it_matters: Explains where to expect problems: eastern wells are more likely to stay fresh, while western users may need to test for saltiness, blend sources, or limit depth.
findings.scope: Confined aquifers across district, east to west

findings.title: Station readings confirm most wells are usable, with a few salty hotspots
findings.statement: May 2017 confined measurements span 400 at Medra and Dehgam-III to 3210 at Nasmed (Kalol) with second-highest 1590 at Dingucha-I; most sites are under 2000, including Bhat-II 410, IsanpurMota-I 440, Aluva 420, Koba 520, Gandhinagar-I 770 and Dharisana 880, while Chhatral 1240, Pundhra-I 1300 and Dingucha-I 1590 stand out higher. Co-located repeats at the same coordinates vary sharply — Bhat-II 410 vs Bhat-I 750, Dingucha-I 1590 vs Dingucha-II 430, and IsanpurMota I/II/III 440/570/820 — indicating different depths or screens.
findings.why_it_matters: For a well owner, the district average matters less than the nearest tube-well: a salty result at Nasmed or Dingucha-I does not mean neighboring Medra or Aluva is salty, and repeat names with different numbers should be checked for depth before use.
findings.scope: 30 confined monitoring stations, May 2017, Gandhinagar 12, Kalol 8, Mansa 6, Dehgam 4

findings.title: Fluoride is the main health-related limit, worst in Dahegam
findings.statement: Fluoride above 1.5 ppm defines problem villages: Dahegam has 9, Gandhinagar taluka 6 (eastern part deteriorates at depth, near Sabarmati), Kalol 2 (shallow poor in south-west) and Mansa 2 (TDS deteriorates at depth while fluoride is higher shallow); Dahegam's east/north-east has limited granular horizons due to 40-100 m clay, limited tube-well depth and reduced yields from over-exploitation, and problem villages are reported to increase every year.
findings.why_it_matters: Fluoride above the limit affects teeth and bones, so these counts point to where drinking water needs testing, treatment or alternate sources first, and the yearly increase signals a growing rather than stable issue.
findings.scope: Unconfined aquifer villages/hamlets by taluka, fluoride >1.5 ppm per GWSSB

findings.title: Shallow groundwater is generally fresh, spanning 350 to 1,320 mg/L
findings.statement: Shallow (unconfined) groundwater across Gandhinagar district ranged from 350 to 1,320 mg/L TDS in May 2017, indicating generally low to moderate mineralisation.
findings.why_it_matters: TDS controls taste and acceptability; knowing the overall range shows that most shallow water is not highly saline but that some wells are distinctly saltier and need attention for drinking use.

findings.title: Freshest pockets at Devkaran-na-muvada, Sanoda and Bilodra
findings.statement: The freshest shallow water was at Devkaran-na-muvada (350 mg/L), Sanoda (410 mg/L) and Bilodra (410 mg/L), with other low values at Koteshwar (490 mg/L), Delvad (500 mg/L) and Karai (580 mg/L).
findings.why_it_matters: These are the most suitable shallow sources from a salinity point of view and are useful reference points for drinking supply and for protecting good-quality recharge areas.
findings.scope: Dehgam and Mansa talukas, plus Koteshwar area

findings.title: Highest dissolved solids at Kadjodra, Hilol and nearby central stations
findings.statement: The highest dissolved solids were at Kadjodra (1,320 mg/L) and Hilol (1,260 mg/L), followed by Antroli (1,130 mg/L), Mubarakpura (1,130 mg/L), Magodi (1,060 mg/L) and Valad (970 mg/L) and Harsoli (890 mg/L).
findings.why_it_matters: Water above about 1,000 mg/L tastes saltier and is more likely to cause complaints or scaling, so these wells should be prioritised for repeat testing and for checking suitability for drinking versus other uses.
findings.scope: Mainly Dehgam Taluka plus Magodi and Mubarakpura

findings.title: A deep basin fill from alluvium to basement
findings.statement: The district sits on Quaternary alluvium (silt, sand, clay, gravel and kankar) over Tertiary Miocene sandstone-shale, Oligocene sandstone-shale-limestone and Eocene shale-siltstone, resting on Cretaceous Deccan Trap basalt and Himatnagar Sandstone above Precambrian basement.
findings.why_it_matters: This layered cake sets the total space available for groundwater — hundreds of metres of porous fill in the west versus thin cover on hard rock in the east.

findings.title: Sediments wedge thickens to the west
findings.statement: Sediments thicken strongly westward: Quaternary cover is under 50 m in the east and over 400 m in the west, Miocene is met at under 50 m in the east and beyond 400 m in the west, with a 5–90 m upper granular zone and a thick grey clay marker at the top of the Miocene; in the east basalt and Himatnagar Sandstone rise to 70–100 m depth.
findings.why_it_matters: Well designers cannot use one depth everywhere — shallow wells work in the east, while only deep wells reach productive sands in the west.

findings.title: Many boreholes correlated into one stacked aquifer system
findings.statement: From 73 drillings (31 exploratory wells plus observation wells, piezometers and a slim hole, drilled 34–614 m), logs were simplified from an initial 3 aquifers to a multiple system A to H: A is phreatic to semi-confined, B to G are confined sands separated by aquitards I–IV and aquicludes V–VI, and H is thick Himatnagar Sandstone; to 611 m, 352 m of post-Miocene (A–E) overlies 259 m of Miocene (F–G).
findings.why_it_matters: Grouping messy sand-clay alternations into named aquifers and clay barriers lets managers talk about the same layers and predict which depth will yield good water.

findings.title: Cross-sections and 3-D model make layers visible
findings.statement: Lithology and electrical logs from CGWB and state wells were correlated by location and depth in RockWorks 16 to build eight transects (for example Khoraj-Dabhi to Pilvai, Kalol to Khadat, Shertha to Giyod), a fence diagram and a 3-D solid model to 300 m showing unconfined aquifer, confined groups 1–3, aquitards 1–3, predominant clay and basalt.
findings.why_it_matters: Maps turn one-dimensional well logs into continuous underground pictures, so users can see where aquifers pinch out, where clays protect them, and where drilling is worthwhile.

findings.title: Shallow aquifer thin, patchy and largely dry
findings.statement: The unconfined (Aquifer-A) layer tapped by dug wells (10–25 m) and shallow tubewells (50–100 m) is thin in the east and thicker in the west, but is now dry over most of the district and forms a usable aquifer only in eastern Dahegam and Gandhinagar talukas and near the Sabarmati River.
findings.why_it_matters: Villages cannot rely on shallow wells except in the northeast and riverine strip; elsewhere supply must come from deeper confined sands.

findings.title: Deep confined sands carry present supply
findings.statement: Aquifers B and C (Confined I and II, within 240 m) are the most exploited and tapped by most tubewells district-wide; Aquifer D (Confined III) is developed in Mansa and Kalol, while E, F, G and the thick Himatnagar H aquifer remain largely for future exploration, with the prolific exploited zone deepening from under 100 m in the east to over 300 m in parts of Mansa.
findings.why_it_matters: Protecting and monitoring the 50–300 m confined zone matters most for water security, and deeper Miocene and sandstone layers offer the main reserve if shallow and intermediate layers fail.

findings.title: A westward-thickening Quaternary to Miocene wedge on basalt
findings.statement: Quaternary alluvium overlies a thick clay bed then alternating Miocene sand, sandstone, siltstone and clay/claystone, with basalts below the Miocene in the east; the whole wedge thickens westward and Miocene is identified by a bluish-grey/grey clay marker, grading upward without a distinct break into buff-yellowish sticky clays and fine-to-very-coarse sands with occasional gravel.
findings.why_it_matters: Westward thickening means far more storage and thicker aquifers in the west, while the shallow eastern basement and marker clay limit deep drilling and help correlate layers across the district.

findings.title: One unconfined plus three confined aquifers separated by clays
findings.statement: Legends consistently show Unconfined Aquifer at top, Aquitards 1, 2 and 3, Confined Aquifer Groups 1, 2 and 3, predominant clay and basalt; sections show lensing, thinning/pinching and clay wedges thickening to the southwest, confirming four regional aquifers separated by clays rather than one continuous sand.
findings.why_it_matters: Separating the stack into four managed units explains why shallow and deep water levels, quality and yields differ and why leakage or connection through clays matters for recharge and contamination.

findings.title: Shallow unconfined aquifer: thin in east, productive but variable
findings.statement: The phreatic aquifer of coarse sand, gravel, pebbles and medium-to-fine clayey sand occurs from surface to 90 m, 15-90 m thick, with water struck at 3-71 m, TDS 500-1300 mg/l and yields of 0.1-12 lps with no reported transmissivity.
findings.why_it_matters: It is the first water met by wells and most vulnerable to pollution and water-table fluctuation; its modest, variable yield and quality guide decisions on shallow irrigation and drinking supply.

findings.title: Deep confined system: thicker sands, higher flows, deeper pressure levels
findings.statement: Confined I (55-150 m, 10-30 m thick, water level 30-115 m, 0.1-30 lps, T 11.35-88 m2/day, generally good quality), Confined II (90-210 m, 10-50 m thick, water level 60-155 m, 1-20 lps, T 39.69-445 m2/day, generally good quality) and Confined III (245-300 m, 15-50 m thick, water level 135-194 m, 1.75-25 lps, T 53.13-237.44 m2/day, variable quality) provide progressively deeper, more pressured but overlapping resources.
findings.why_it_matters: Deeper zones offer larger, more reliable tubewell yields for towns and industry, but greater depth, higher lift, and variable quality in the deepest zone raise cost and treatment considerations.

findings.title: A small, densely settled capital district
findings.statement: Gandhinagar District is a compact capital district of 2,163 sq km with 4 talukas and 252 villages and about 1.39 million people in 2011, including the state capital and suburbs such as Chandkheda, Motera and Adalaj.
findings.why_it_matters: A large population and capital-city functions are packed into a small area, so drinking-water, urban and farm demands all converge on the same groundwater system.

findings.title: Flat alluvial land that stores water underground
findings.statement: The whole district is North Gujarat alluvial plain with no hills, lying at 56-126 m amsl between 22°56'-23°36' N and 72°23'-73°05' E. Predominant geology is Alluvium/Tertiaries and the major water-bearing formation is Quaternary alluvium.
findings.why_it_matters: Without hills or large surface reservoirs, water security depends on sands and gravels beneath the plain to store and transmit groundwater.

findings.title: A big river that is now seasonal
findings.statement: The Sabarmati is the principal river flowing north-south along eastern Mansa near Mahudi and through central Gandhinagar taluka, with Khari and Meshwo as other drainages. The Sabarmati was once perennial but is now generally dry in lean months except for Dharoi releases and Narmada water retained downstream of the canal, with high banks up to 60 m upstream and a broad sandy, winding bed downstream.
findings.why_it_matters: A dry-season river means villages and farms cannot rely on surface flow for much of the year, increasing pressure on wells and making river recharge and canal seepage critical to sustain levels.

findings.title: Short monsoon, long dry demand
findings.statement: Climate is semi-arid with rains concentrated in June-September southwest monsoon (~95% of annual rain, July heaviest), hot summers peaking in May, cool winters November-February and high evaporation demand. The district has no climatological station, so Ahmedabad Airport (55 m amsl, 23°04'N 72°38'E) is used as representative.
findings.why_it_matters: Recharge happens in a 3-4 month window while heat and crops draw water most of the year; a weak monsoon quickly translates into deeper wells and falling levels.

findings.title: Sandy soils farmed almost everywhere
findings.statement: Sandy loam is the major soil and farming dominates land use: 1,545 sq km net sown versus only 24 sq km forest, with 233 sq km uncultivable, 1,438 sq km cultivable and 243 sq km waste as tabulated. Kharif, rabi and summer crops are grown, including rice, bajra, wheat, jowar, maize, mung, groundnut, mustard, cotton, tobacco and fennel.
findings.why_it_matters: Permeable sandy loam lets monsoon rain soak in, but near-total cultivation means that recharge opportunity is matched by very high crop water need.

findings.title: An irrigation economy built on wells
findings.statement: Irrigation is overwhelmingly from groundwater — 2,328 dug wells and 2,203 tubewells (818 deep + 1,385 shallow) compared with 1 tank/pond structure, 1 canal and 3 other sources. Net irrigated area of 642 sq km yields a gross irrigated area of 1,438 sq km, indicating double and triple cropping.
findings.why_it_matters: With almost no surface irrigation infrastructure counted, repeated yearly cropping depends on pumping; this intensity explains why extraction later exceeds replenishment and levels fall.

findings.title: A small four-taluka district on the North Gujarat plain
findings.statement: Gandhinagar District is a compact North Gujarat plain district made up of four talukas — Gandhinagar, Dahegam, Kalol and Mansa — covered by Survey of India toposheets 46A/7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 15 and 16.
findings.why_it_matters: A small administrative area with four distinct farming units means groundwater stress and solutions vary taluka to taluka, not just district-wide.
findings.scope: Gandhinagar District and its four talukas

findings.title: Many people on little land — and still growing
findings.statement: In 2011 the district held 1,387,478 people at 660 persons per sq km, growing 12.15% over 2001-2011, with a sex ratio of 920 females per 1,000 males and 85.78% literacy.
findings.why_it_matters: High density plus town, capital-city and village drinking-water needs compete directly with irrigation for the same groundwater.

findings.title: Hot most of the year, wet for only three months
findings.statement: The climate is hot and strongly seasonal: May peaks around 41.8°C, August humidity reaches 79%, and rain is concentrated in June-September — July 265.3 mm, August 219.8 mm and September 171.9 mm — with almost nothing from November to May. No station exists inside the district, so Ahmedabad IMD station (23°04'N, 72°38'E) is used as proxy, and its 799.6 mm annual total differs from the 739 mm normal quoted in the text.
findings.why_it_matters: A 3-4 month recharge window must sustain 12 months of drinking and irrigation demand, making storage in soil and aquifers and dry-season pumping decisive.
findings.scope: Gandhinagar District proxied by Ahmedabad IMD station

findings.title: Rivers in the east, little natural drainage in the west
findings.statement: The Sabarmati drains north to south through Mansa and Gandhinagar talukas. The Khari (about 40 km of its 160 km in this district) flows through northwestern Dahegam and southeastern Gandhinagar to Vahelal toward Ahmedabad; the Meshwo follows Dahegam's northeastern border from Rajasthan, entering at Sahebnamubada and leaving at Kuha; the Vatrak touches Dahegam's southeastern border for a few km. The report highlights as key features the lack of any definite natural drainage in the west and the Narmada Canal System as artificial drainage.
findings.why_it_matters: Where rivers are absent, rainfall cannot concentrate and recharge naturally, increasing reliance on canals, tanks and groundwater to carry water to fields and wells.

findings.title: Two soil worlds: tight saline clays west, open sandy loams elsewhere
findings.statement: Western soils are alkaline and saline, deep grey calcareous sandy clay loam with very low permeability, while the rest of the district is sandy loam, light grey to brown, generally deep with moderate to good permeability and drainage (UNDP assessment).
findings.why_it_matters: Low-permeability saline soils in the west limit how much rain soaks down to aquifers and raise waterlogging and salinity risks when canal water or groundwater is applied.

findings.title: Three-quarters farmed — and cropped twice
findings.statement: About 76% of the district (164,954 ha net sown) is farmed, with gross cropping of 217,228 ha and 132% cropping intensity because 106,796 ha is sown more than once. Forest is only 2,044 ha (under 1%). Intensity varies sharply: Dahegam reaches 183%, Kalol 182% and Gandhinagar 170%, while Mansa is only 116%, reflecting different access to water and double-cropping.
findings.why_it_matters: Double-cropping on three-quarters of the land locks in dry-season water demand long after monsoon recharge ends, putting the burden on groundwater and canals.

findings.title: A diversified, year-round crop calendar that outlasts the rains
findings.statement: Farming spans all three seasons within a 20 June to 30 October-15 November rainy window: kharif (144,540 ha, led by grass 47,523 ha, divela/castor 28,546 ha and cotton 23,702 ha), rabi (71,420 ha, led by paddy dharu 28,682 ha, grass, potato and vegetables) and summer (about 22,912 ha stated, led by grass, bajri and vegetables). Wheat (25%), cotton (22%) and rapeseed-castor (21%) dominate the major-crop pie, with bajri, guvar, groundnut, tobacco, fennel and paddy filling diverse niches; cotton sown in June is harvested in December-February and wheat sown in November-December in March, so fields need water months after rains end.
findings.why_it_matters: High-value, water-demanding crops in rabi and summer — paddy, potato, vegetables, tobacco, cotton — can only succeed with reliable irrigation, directly linking farm incomes to groundwater levels and canal supplies.

findings.title: Flat alluvial plain with three rivers
findings.statement: The district has monotonous flat topography drained by the Sabarmati, Meshwo and Khari rivers, and forms part of the Cambay basin occupied by Quaternary alluvium comprising silt and sand.
findings.why_it_matters: Flat terrain and alluvial silt-sand explain why farming could spread widely and why productive aquifers exist underneath — but also why natural drainage and runoff capture are limited without storage and recharge.

findings.title: Semi-arid climate with modest rainfall
findings.statement: The district has a semi-arid climate with annual normal rainfall of 744 mm.
findings.why_it_matters: With less than 750 mm in a normal year to support intensive double-cropping, the district must bridge long dry periods with groundwater, making rainfall variability a direct farming risk.

findings.title: Dry-season cropping signals irrigation dependence, but totals are unreliable
findings.statement: Source tables report summer cropping including Kalol at 3,585 ha (3-year average 4,250 ha), but the Mansa summer entry (~14,879 ha stated vs ~7,081 ha summed from components including 5,119 ha grass) and the stated district summer total (22,912 ha) are flagged as internally inconsistent and should not be used without qualification.
findings.why_it_matters: Summer crops can only survive on irrigation, so even a few thousand hectares confirm dry-season pressure on wells. The inconsistency flag matters because planning for that pressure needs corrected, consistent taluka crop statistics.
findings.scope: Kalol and Mansa talukas; district summer total

findings.title: Monsoon lifts the shallowest ground most
findings.statement: The same two wells bookend both seasons: Dahegam is shallowest and Mubarak Pura deepest in May and November 2017. The shallow end recovers strongly with the monsoon, rising from 9.45 to 3.03 mbgl (about 6.4 m of recovery), while the deep end barely changes from 72.20 to 71.20 mbgl (about 1 m). The reported zonal map stays identical: 10-50 mbgl in Kalol and Dahegam and 50-70 mbgl in central Gandhinagar, northwest Kalol and northern Mansa.
findings.why_it_matters: For a household or farmer, this means rain relief is uneven. Where water is already near the surface a good monsoon can bring it within a few metres; where it is 70 m down, one monsoon does not bring it back, so deep wells stay expensive to pump.
findings.scope: Phreatic/unconfined wells district-wide, May 2017 pre-monsoon vs November 2017 post-monsoon; extrema at Dahegam and Mubarak Pura

findings.title: Water sits deeper toward the northwest and moves west
findings.statement: Depth grows from east/south to northwest/north in every layer. Shallow water is 10-50 m in eastern and western Kalol-Dahegam but 50-70 m in the centre, northwest and north. Confined Aquifer I averages 30-70 m in eastern Gandhinagar-Dahegam and southern Kalol, 70-110 m in western Kalol and northern Mansa, and over 110 m in northwestern Kalol. Aquifer II is deeper still at 50-130 m in the east/south, 130-150 m in northwestern Kalol and Mansa, and over 150 m at the northern extreme. The November 2017 water-table elevation falls from east to west, indicating general groundwater flow from east to west.
findings.why_it_matters: Location predicts cost and risk. Northwestern Kalol and northern Mansa face the deepest pumping lifts and the largest declines, while flow direction tells planners where recharge upstream protects wells downstream.
findings.scope: District-wide phreatic May/Nov 2017 and decadal pre-monsoon averages 2009-2018 for Confined Aquifer I and II

findings.title: Shallow wells are mixed, deep wells mostly fall
findings.statement: From 2008-2017 the shallow aquifer is split: about half the wells fall at -0.04 to -0.93 m/year (for example Kadjodra -0.9286, Jindva -0.7897, Bilodra -0.7886) and half rise at +0.02 to +3.77 m/year (Valad +0.0229, Amrapur +3.7671). Confined Group-I almost all falls, with the largest falls at Pethapur Pz-II -5.03, Isanpur Mota-II -2.21, Adraj Moti -1.54 and Koba -1.07 m/year, against small rises at Indroda +1.36 and Nasmed +1.30. Confined Group-II, described as most developed for irrigation, also falls at most stations - Dingucha-II -1.74, Rancharada -1.61, Bhoyan Moti -1.50, Chiloda Pz-II -1.19, Adalaj Pz-I -1.05, Kharna-III -0.76, Dehgam-I -0.24 - with only Pundhara-II +0.45 and Kalol Rep Pz-II +0.0385 rising.
findings.why_it_matters: Averaging hides the problem. The shallow layer can still recover in places, but the deep irrigation layers are dropping year after year, so wells that tap them must be deepened and use more energy even in normal rainfall years.
findings.scope: Village/station trends 2008-2017 pre- and post-monsoon combined: unconfined ~27 sites, Confined Group-I 24 sites, Confined Group-II 15 sites

findings.title: Years of pumping above recharge have lowered the system
findings.statement: Aquifers I and II tapped together are developed in most of the district, are the most exploited, and water levels are described as declining at an alarming rate. About 80% of the district shows steadier decline over the years with falling piezometric heads, deeper well depths, lower yields and large-scale development. Assessed development was 184% in 2004, 165% in 2009, 145% in 2011 and 2013, and 113.55% in 2017 - still above 100%, meaning use above recharge. Farmers are reported to increase pump settings by about 3 m (10 ft) every year, while a CGWB test showed about 20 m submergence is enough for about 10 litres per second, so heads must be tracked in space and time.
findings.why_it_matters: Even the improvement from 184% to 113% still means over-use. The yearly 3-metre pump lowering is the household cost of that imbalance - higher electricity, deeper drilling and wells that can go dry if heads keep falling.
findings.scope: Gandhinagar district, confined Aquifers I and II tapped together; development assessments 2004-2017

findings.title: Rivers, canals and a few villages buck the decline
findings.statement: Against the regional fall, shallow piezometers near the Sabarmati River and Narmada Main Canal show rises in places, and several village trends rise: for example Sanoda +0.98, Rakhiyal +1.15, Hilol reported rise, Delvad +0.33 and Dahegam-II +0.48 in the unconfined record. Even in confined Group-I a few stations rise (Indroda +1.36, Amrapur Pz-II +1.07, Shertha +0.35) and hydrographs such as Koba-Pz at 55-75 mbgl and Rangpur-Pz-II at 100-120 mbgl with May-October measurements show the seasonal saw-tooth on a falling baseline.
findings.why_it_matters: These exceptions point to solutions. Where river or canal seepage reaches the aquifer, levels can stabilise or recover, suggesting that protecting recharge corridors and spreading that recharge could slow decline elsewhere.
findings.scope: Shallow piezometers near Sabarmati River and Narmada Main Canal and selected confined stations 2008-2017

findings.title: A split post-monsoon: half the shallow wells still below normal
findings.statement: October 2017 did not lift all shallow wells equally: five Dehgam wells were 1.5 to 8.3 m deeper than their 2007-2016 October average, while four were 1.1 to 2.2 m shallower, showing a split between lingering deficit and short-term recovery.
findings.why_it_matters: A single post-monsoon reading can mislead; comparing it to the decadal average shows which villages banked recharge and which entered the dry season already in deficit and will face higher pumping costs.
findings.scope: Dehgam Taluka shallow unconfined wells Sr.1-10, October decadal average vs October 2017

findings.title: Deep aquifers on a downward escalator, except Kalol
findings.statement: Deeper confined levels fell steadily from 2008 to 2017 at Chiloda (-1.19), Dahegam-I (-1.14), Palaj (-3.14) and Pethapur (-5.13), with only Kalol Rep Pz-II rising (+0.39).
findings.why_it_matters: Steady multi-year falls in confined aquifers signal that pumping exceeds replenishment; wells must go deeper over time and the Kalol exception suggests local recharge or reduced draft can reverse the pattern.
findings.scope: Confined Aquifer Group-II, 2008-2017 village trend wells across Gandhinagar district

findings.title: From comfortable to critical: water-table geography
findings.statement: Water-table elevations derived as ground level minus 2017 depth range from about 62 m at Rakhiyal and 48.7 m at Sanoda down to 20.8 m at Mubarakpura, 13.4 m at Bhat-II and -2 m at Valad, where water sits below sea-level datum.
findings.why_it_matters: Elevation puts depth into landscape context; very low or negative water tables flag areas where wells are most vulnerable to drying, seawater intrusion risk, and where recharge protection matters most.
findings.scope: District-wide unconfined stations Sr.11-20, ground elevation minus October 2017 depth

findings.title: Volatile years hide inside the average
findings.statement: The decade was not smooth: Sanoda spiked to 55.2 m in 2011-2012 before recovering to 33.3 m in 2017 (+5.16 m fluctuation), while Jindva deepened from 28.5 m in 2007 to ~36 m after 2011 and stayed deep (-2.55 m fluctuation).
findings.why_it_matters: Big swings mean planning on an average alone is risky; storage, crop choice and drinking-water backup must handle the worst years, not just the mean.
findings.scope: Decadal October series 2007-2016 for Sanoda, Jindva and Hilol

findings.title: Deep monitoring mirrors the shallow method
findings.statement: The district maintains a separate Confined-I ledger for 15 alluvium wells drilled 100-150 m deep with ground elevations 51-113 m, reporting decadal average, May 2017 dry-season level, fluctuation and water table in the same arithmetic as the shallow ledger.
findings.why_it_matters: Having a parallel dry-season record for the heavily pumped 100-150 m zone lets managers see whether deep pumping is stabilizing or mining storage, which shallow monsoon wells alone cannot reveal.
findings.scope: Annexure-2 Confined Aquifer-I 100-150 m district network

findings.title: Two water worlds: shallow fringe versus deep confined pressure
findings.statement: Shallow alluvial wells record water only ~9-13 m below ground (drilled 21-67 m), while Confined-I wells average ~42-119 m depth to water (drilled 100-150 m). Paliya varies 8.94-13.69 m and Serthapara1 9.1-13.42 m, versus Dingucha-I 118.43 m and Adraj Moti 111.68 m averages.
findings.why_it_matters: Shallow water can recover quickly after monsoon but is vulnerable to drying; deep water is the main supply for sustained pumping and its large depth shows high lift costs and slow recovery if depleted.
findings.scope: 5 shallow alluvial stations (Dahegam-II, Kasturinagar, Lodra, Paliya, Serthapara1) vs district confined network

findings.title: May 2017 sat below the decade mean across much of Confined-I
findings.statement: Most Confined-I wells were deeper in May 2017 than their decadal mean. Adraj Moti (-8.22 m), Koba (-6.41 m), Bhat-I (-3.03 m), Shertha (-2.4 m) and Isanpur Mota-II (-2.25 m) all fell, while only Indroda (+3.79 m), Nasmed (+2.39 m) and Kharna-I (+1.71 m) were notably shallower.
findings.why_it_matters: A pre-monsoon month sitting below the 10-year mean is a classic sign of a falling pressure surface from sustained pumping, meaning wells must pump from greater depth each year.
findings.scope: 15 Confined-I stations in Kalol, Mansa and Gandhinagar talukas, decadal average vs May 2017

findings.title: Deepest drops cluster in Confined-II, up to ~19 m below average
findings.statement: Confined-II also fell: Pethapur Pz-I -18.69 m, Dahegam (Dehgam) I at 65 m elevation -14.48 m, Rancharada -11.7 m, Adalaj Pz-I -7.94 m, Dingucha-II -7.82 m, Gandhinagar town -7.5 m, Chiloda Pz-II -7.21 m and Chiloda Pz-I -6.85 m. Year series show steady deepening, e.g. Gandhinagar 97.9 m in 2007 to 106.9 m in 2017 and Kharna-III ~151.25 m to 161.3 m.
findings.why_it_matters: Drops of 7-19 m in the main 180-240 m deep supply aquifer mean sharply higher energy costs and risk that wells go dry or turn brackish if the trend continues.
findings.scope: 18 Confined-II stations with May 2007-2016 series, decadal average vs May 2017

findings.title: Not everywhere is falling — pockets of stability and rise
findings.statement: A minority held steady or rose: Pundhara-II 0.06 m, Charada Pz-II 0.73 m, Dehgam-I 1.1 m, Amrapur Pzi 2.05 m and Kalol Rep Pz-II 3.62 m shallower than average in Confined-II, and Indroda, Nasmed, Limbodara and Dingucha-I near-stable in Confined-I.
findings.why_it_matters: Stable spots show that recharge, geology or lower pumping can protect levels; they are natural guides for where managed recharge and pumping controls are most likely to work.
findings.scope: Stable or rising pockets in Mansa, Dehgam, Gandhinagar and Kalol

findings.title: Same village, different depths — a stacked aquifer
findings.statement: Villages with two wells at almost identical coordinates but different drilled depths record different but both-deep levels: Isanpur Mota-I (120 m) averages 92 m vs Isanpur Mota-II (150 m) 112.65 m; Chiloda Pz-I (200 m) 106.49 m vs Chiloda Pz-II (167 m) 106.24 m; Paliya and Dahegam-II share lat 23.17 lon 72.84 but are separate sites.
findings.why_it_matters: It tells drillers and planners that depth alone does not guarantee better water; each layer has its own pressure and decline rate and must be monitored separately.
findings.scope: Co-located nested wells at Isanpur Mota, Chiloda, Paliya/Dahegam-II and Dehgam area

findings.title: Most deep wells sit far down and drift deeper over ten years
findings.statement: The long Confined-II records for villages like Dingucha-II, Kharna-III, Bhoyan Moti and Rancharada show persistently deep water and a dominant falling trend over 2007-2017, with some series complete and others starting only in 2012.
findings.why_it_matters: Deep, falling levels mean pumping lifts, costs and risks grow, and there is less buffer in dry years. Complete series like Gandhinagar and Isanpur Mota-III are the benchmarks for judging whether management is stabilizing the system.

findings.title: Steepest declines point to over-development hotspots
findings.statement: The steepest decadal drops cluster around Dahegam-I at -14.48 m and Pethapur Pz-I at -18.69 m, where Pethapur jumps from about 78.5 m in 2013 to about 106.5 m in 2014.
findings.why_it_matters: Such large, localized drops are classic signs that withdrawals exceed recharge. They flag where regulation, reduced pumping or added recharge is most urgent, and where the sudden jump should be verified before decisions are made.

findings.title: A few rises and a steady well show recharge can work locally
findings.statement: Against the falling background, Dehgam-I shows a +1.1 m rise in one compilation, Kalol Rep Pz-II shows a +3.62 m rise, and Palaj Pz-I holds steady at about 99.5 m average and 99.5 m in 2017.
findings.why_it_matters: Rises near rivers, canals or recharge areas prove decline is not inevitable. These spots are natural laboratories for what helps - seepage, good monsoon intake or lighter pumping - and can guide where to replicate recharge.

findings.title: Paired wells at the same village unlock depth-by-depth insight
findings.statement: At places like Dehgam-II at 135 m depth versus Dehgam-III at 97 m at essentially the same coordinates, and at Chiloda Pz-I versus Pz-II and Palaj and Pethapur pairs, managers deliberately watch different depths side by side, while Confined-I examples like Rangpur-II around 110-111 m and Dharisana extend the picture to the shallower confined zone.
findings.why_it_matters: Without pairs you cannot tell if a drop is only shallow or affects the whole system. Paired data helps decide which depth can still be safely pumped and where to screen new wells.

findings.title: Seasonal snapshots and flow direction frame the decadal story
findings.statement: The program uses May 2017 for before-monsoon depth and November 2017 for after-monsoon depth, with a November 2017 flow interpretation showing a general east-to-west movement to separate seasonal recharge from the long-term trend.
findings.why_it_matters: A single measurement can mislead after a good rain or heavy pumping. Comparing pre- and post-monsoon levels and knowing which way water flows tells whether a rise is just seasonal recovery or real long-term improvement.

findings.title: Same alluvium, different layer cake
findings.statement: Dahegam has three aquifer groups — phreatic 0-45 mbgl, Confined-I 55-85 mbgl and Confined-II 90-110 mbgl with no Confined-III — while Gandhinagar has four groups — phreatic 0-70 mbgl, Confined-I 115-150 mbgl, Confined-II 175-200 mbgl and Confined-III 245-300 mbgl. Both are rated suitable for drinking and irrigation.
findings.why_it_matters: A well that is adequate in Dahegam at 90-110 m would still be in the upper system in Gandhinagar, where the main confined targets lie 100-200 m deeper. That controls drilling cost, pump size and which villages can reach the deeper reserves.

findings.title: What the wells actually measure
findings.statement: Direct well summaries show phreatic sands (coarse sand, gravel, pebbles with medium-fine and clayey sand, Recent to Miocene) 15-45 m thick in Dahegam and 15-70 m thick in Gandhinagar, yielding 0.1-12 litres per second with TDS 500-1300 mg/l and variable quality. Confined-I (medium-coarse sand and gravel with sandy clay, 10-30 m thick) yields up to 30 lps with TDS 500-2000 mg/l; Confined-II (fine-medium sand, 10-20 m in Dahegam and 10-25 m in Gandhinagar) yields 1-20 lps. Only Gandhinagar has a documented Confined-III (medium sand, 15-50 m thick, water level 135-194 mbgl, 1.75-25 lps).
findings.why_it_matters: Thickness, water level and yield tell a non-specialist whether water is shallow and low-yielding or deep and more productive, and why the deeper Gandhinagar zones need higher-lift pumps but can give larger discharges.

findings.title: The Blue clay line not to cross
findings.statement: Both block narratives use Blue clay (Tertiary) as the marker between the Quaternary system above and the Tertiary system below, and both warn that tube wells below the Blue clay give relatively poor quality and higher-temperature water. Groundwater is described as predominantly potable for domestic, drinking, irrigation and industrial use, with fluoride above permissible limits in a few samples but no major health issue attributed because drinking supply uses Narmada Canal water.
findings.why_it_matters: The clay is a practical stop sign for drillers: going deeper than the mapped Quaternary confined zones risks saltier, warmer water that is not worth the extra drilling, and explains why quality management focuses on the mapped I, II and III zones.

findings.title: Over-used today, efficiency as the only new water
findings.statement: On a 2017 assessment basis Dahegam extracts 14805.82 ham against 13926.81 ham availability (106.31%) and Gandhinagar extracts 13859.66 ham against 13323.67 ham (104.02%), leaving zero net availability for future use. No new check dams or percolation tanks are recommended because the 2013 master-plan runoff (3.16 MCM in Dahegam, 4.38 MCM in Gandhinagar) is already committed — 108 structures holding 5.8 MCM in Dahegam and 503 structures holding 25.4 MCM in Gandhinagar. Demand-side micro-irrigation (9932 ha more in Dahegam, 11392 ha more in Gandhinagar) is calculated to cut draft enough to move both blocks from Over-Exploited to Critical.
findings.why_it_matters: With supply-side recharge exhausted, the only quantified path to sustainability in these blocks is using less water per hectare through drip and sprinkler, which matters for farm subsidies, canal-water conjunctive use and future allocation planning.
findings.scope: Dahegam and Gandhinagar groundwater balance 2017 basis

findings.title: Two neighbours, slightly different stacks
findings.statement: Kalol and Mansa share the same four zones — phreatic plus Confined I, II and III, all rated suitable for drinking and irrigation — but the depths shift: Kalol phreatic 0–90 m, I 110–150 m, II 165–190 m, III 240–300 m; Mansa phreatic 0–70 m, I 100–150 m, II 185–210 m, III 260–300 m, with Gandhinagar taluka intermediate at 0–70 / 115–150 / 175–200 / 245–300 m.
findings.why_it_matters: A driller or farmer cannot copy a successful well depth from one taluka to the next; the same good aquifer is 20–30 m deeper or shallower across the boundary, which controls cost, yield and quality.
findings.scope: Kalol Taluka vs Mansa Taluka aquifer occurrence depths

findings.title: A four-storey building with a Blue-clay floor
findings.statement: The report describes four multi-layered sand-and-clay groups: coarse sand, gravel, pebbles and clayey sand at the top, then medium-to-coarse sand and gravel, fine-to-medium sand, and medium sand interbedded with sandy clay below, all Recent to Miocene. A Blue clay (Tertiary) marker separates Quaternary from Tertiary, and wells drilled below it yield relatively poor quality and comparatively higher temperature water, with tube-well depths deepening from ~100 m in the east to >300 m in the west.
findings.why_it_matters: The clay layers are what make deeper water confined and often better protected but harder to recharge; punching through the Blue clay does not find more fresh water, it finds saltier, warmer water.
findings.scope: District-wide Quaternary Alluvium Older and Younger Alluvium system

findings.title: Deeper water, bigger yields, saltier edges
findings.statement: Water gets deeper and wells get stronger with depth, but saltiness spreads at the bottom: phreatic levels 14–71 m in Kalol and 31–65 m in Mansa with TDS 500–1300 and yields 0.1–12 lps; Confined I levels 39–117 m (Kalol) and 38–110 m (Mansa) with TDS 500–2000 and up to 30 lps; Confined II levels 54–152 m to 100–161 m with transmissivity up to 445 m2/day; Confined III levels 135–160 m to 135–194 m with TDS up to 2980 and remark variable water quality versus generally good above.
findings.why_it_matters: Shallow wells are cheapest but most variable and vulnerable to decline; deep wells can give 20–25 lps but risk brackish water near 3000 mg/l TDS, so fluoride exceedances and variable quality matter even though Narmada canal water currently avoids a drinking-water health crisis.
findings.scope: Phreatic through Confined III in Kalol, Mansa and Gandhinagar talukas
findings.pattern_type: depth-dependent level, yield and quality gradient

findings.title: Over-used today, different rescue paths
findings.statement: Both blocks pump more than they receive: Kalol availability 11,137 ham vs draft 12,700 ham (114% Over-exploited, 33,851 ham including in-storage); Mansa 8,620 ham vs 12,012 ham (139% Over-exploited, 23,912 ham including in-storage) with zero net water for future use. Supply-side recharge is exhausted — 97 check dams + 3 percolation tanks in Kalol (5.15 MCM) and 134 + 56 in Mansa (12.3 MCM) already use the 2.31 and 2.19 MCM non-committed runoff. Demand-side micro-irrigation on ~12,944 ha in Kalol could save 19.42 MCM and bring stage to 99.6% Critical; the same on ~12,459 ha in Mansa saves 18.69 MCM but stage stays 122.3% Over-exploited.
findings.why_it_matters: No new dams will help because surplus runoff is gone; saving water on the farm through micro-irrigation is the only lever, and it is enough to pull Kalol back from the brink but not enough for more-stressed Mansa, which needs additional controls on pumping.
findings.scope: Kalol and Mansa block resource and micro-irrigation scenarios

findings.title: What the drill actually saw
findings.statement: The synthesis rests on named wells: Khoraj Dabhi EWI-II exploratory well, unconfined stations like Hilol, Dharisana, Antroli, Harsoli, Patnakuva and Sanoda, and confined stations like Nasmed and Dingucha I and II. Lithologs spell out the stack metre by metre — for example Gram Bharti 0–40 m sorted sand, Chiloda 15–30 m sand with kankar and 30–42 m feldspar-quartz sand and 192–201 m sand, Giyod 42–52 m fine sand under 52–116 m quartzite sand with clay lenses, Kalol piezometer 53.9–60.8 m pure sand and 108–135 m fine sand with gravel and 189–202 m fine-to-coarse sand, Pore-Gandhinagar 147–156 m coarse sand with gravel, and a 82–235 m clay aquitard at Moti Bardoli — showing why aquifers are thin sands between thick clays.
findings.why_it_matters: These metre-scale logs let a reader trust the block averages: the high yields and variable quality are not guesses but reflect real sand lenses that appear and disappear, and thick clays that seal one aquifer from another.
findings.scope: Exploratory, piezometer, inventory and monitoring wells with depth-wise logs

findings.title: Mansa gives the clearest four-layer local profile
findings.statement: Mansa is documented as a four-zone system: phreatic 0-70 m, Confined I 100-150 m, Confined II 185-210 m in the summary, and Confined III 260-300 m, each listed as suitable for drinking and irrigation.
findings.why_it_matters: It tells a well owner or planner which depth they are actually tapping; a 60-m well and a 280-m well are in completely different aquifers with different levels and quality, so block averages cannot be applied to a single well.

findings.title: Deeper zones sit lower, yield more variably, and vary more in quality
findings.statement: With depth, static water levels get markedly deeper — roughly 38-110 m in Aquifer I, 100-161 m in Aquifer II, and 135-194 m in Aquifer III — while yields and transmissivity widen upward (Aquifer I 0.1-30 lps and T 11.35-88; Aquifer II 1-20 lps and T 39.69-445; Aquifer III 1.75-25 lps and T 53.13-237.44) and the top of the quality range gets saltier, to 2980 mg/L TDS in Aquifer III described as variable.
findings.why_it_matters: Deeper drilling can access thicker, more productive sands but means higher pumping lifts and a greater chance of brackish water; the blue-clay Tertiary marker noted in the text is the practical warning that quality and temperature can change below it.

findings.title: Nested exploratory wells prove the zones are vertically separate
findings.statement: Exploration was done as nested wells at the same village with different screen sets: Mahudi EW-I taps 169-209 m while EW-II/III tap 74-108 m; Pore EW-I taps 234-299 m while EW-II taps 322-385 m; Khoraj-Dabhi EW-IV taps 59-121 m while EW-II taps 253-308 m and EW-III taps 142-223 m; Bardoli EWI taps seven deep slots 238-291 m while EWII taps 54-84 m.
findings.why_it_matters: Without separate screens you cannot tell which layer is falling or turning salty; the nests let testers compare shallow versus deep behaviour side-by-side and choose the right screen for a production well, as at Lakroda 76-88 and 104-116 m or Khadat 76-82, 86-89, 108-120, 128-131 m.

findings.title: Piezometers mirror the exploration nests for level and quality tracking
findings.statement: The piezometer annexure extends the same nested logic for long-term watching: Adalaj Pz-I/II/III at 200, 138 and 47 m; Amrapur Pz-I with screens 162-198 m, Pz-II with 85-144 m, and Pz-III with 36-69 m; Boru Pz-I with 139-169 m versus Pz-II with 28-74 m; Chiloda Pz-I with 172-196 m versus Pz-II with 112-148 m; Kalol Pz-I with 150-192 m versus Pz-II with 36-61 m, plus Sanoda, Dehgam, Gandhinagar and Nardipur stations.
findings.why_it_matters: Paired shallow-deep piezometers are what reveal whether decline is confined to the deep confined system or also affects the water table, guiding where to restrict deep pumping and where shallow recharge can help.

findings.title: Totals are arithmetic but locations and some depths need cleaning before local use
findings.statement: The synthesis rests on a stated total of 23911.96 ham (8619.96 ham dynamic plus 15292 ham in-storage), but the well tables that support it have coarse 2-decimal coordinates spanning about 72.20-72.92 E and 22.99-23.50 N with no datum, one #VALUE! latitude, garbled depth strings like 35311. and 20267., abandoned entries marked Abon/Abnd at Delwada EW-I and Sampa, and a direct conflict on Aquifer II top (85 m in detail versus 185 m in summary).
findings.why_it_matters: A village plan should not navigate by these coordinates alone or order a rig to an exact garbled depth; the numbers are reliable for block-scale comparison, but siting needs field verification, datum confirmation, and resolution of which Aquifer II top applies at that spot.

findings.title: Deep private irrigation wells with deep water levels in the west
findings.statement: Private irrigation tube wells around Kalol, Jalund, Sardhav, Rupal, Unava and Randheja are deep (typically 183-259 m, up to 274 m) and in July 2015 had very deep static levels, roughly 98 to 195 m below the pump.
findings.why_it_matters: Pumping from 100-200 m depth costs more energy and signals a thick unsaturated zone above the tapped aquifer; domestic wells in the same villages cannot be assumed to behave the same way.

findings.title: Dahegam's village supply wells look very different
findings.statement: Dahegam inventory wells are almost all Public/Panchayat domestic wells inside villages near tanks and temples, with highly variable depths from about 46 m at river-bank sites to 457-610 m at Moti-Machhang, Kalyanji-Muwada, Tharakua and Siyavada, and static levels are blank for supply wells — only four GWRDC piezometers report levels around 29-47 m.
findings.why_it_matters: Management for drinking-water security in Dahegam cannot borrow water-level values from Kalol irrigation wells; without levels, drawdown and sustainability cannot be judged from this inventory alone.

findings.title: Nested piezometers were built to see layers separately
findings.statement: At Pethapur (I 200 m, II 122 m, III 55 m), Palaj (I 200 m, II 110 m, III 65 m), Adalaj (I 200 m, II 138 m, III 47 m) and Sardhav (I 451 m, II 331 m, III 200 m) the department built depth-decreasing nests with non-overlapping screens to profile head and quality separately by zone.
findings.why_it_matters: Nests let managers tell whether decline or salinity is shallow or deep, so a falling deep head does not get mistaken for a drying shallow aquifer and vice versa.
findings.scope: Pethapur, Palaj, Adalaj, Sardhav piezometer nests

findings.title: One village, several aquifers stacked in clay
findings.statement: Exploratory wells prove multiple separated productive zones under one village: Pore shallow 234-299 m over deep 322-385 m; Khoraj-Dabhi IV 59-121 m, III 142-223 m, II 253-308 m, I 324-336 m; Galuden-I with ten screens 181-290 m; Chhalla-II, Sanoda, Khadat, Chiloda and Lakroda each with 4-6 narrow screens between about 54 and 198 m.
findings.why_it_matters: Well success depends on hitting the right thin sand band and sealing off the rest; drilling deeper does not always mean more water, and screens must match the intended zone to avoid mixing.

findings.title: What the inventory does not tell us
findings.statement: Only Sr.1-15 have coordinates for mapping; all Dahegam public wells from Sr.16 onward lack coordinates, diameters and static levels, one Amrapur latitude is recorded as #VALUE!, and every well is labelled simply Alluvial, so sand-versus-clay detail is lost in the inventory table.
findings.why_it_matters: Maps, cross-sections and trend analysis built only from this table would be biased to Kalol-Gandhinagar 2015 irrigation wells; Dahegam domestic wells need fresh levels, locations and lithologs before decisions.

findings.title: What the village well list actually records
findings.statement: The well inventory is dominated by public domestic tube-wells 121-183 m deep in alluvium visited 26-31 July 2014 and 9-13 July 2015, with a tail of very shallow 45-61 m river-bank wells and one 17-m dug-well, plus GWRDC piezometers reserved for monitoring.
findings.why_it_matters: It shows everyday supply depends on drilling well past 100 m into alluvial sands, not on shallow open wells — so cost, power and deep-water sustainability decide access.
findings.scope: Gandhinagar District - Gandhinagar, Dehgaon/Dahegam and Kalol talukas

findings.title: Shallow watchers versus deep producers at the same place
findings.statement: Rest water levels separate into two families: 29-47 m in shallow piezometers versus 103-195 m in deep production tube-wells, with Dehgaon itself offering a 17-m dug-well, 121-137-m tube-wells and a 102.42-m piezometer at the same place.
findings.why_it_matters: The gap proves layered aquifers: a shallow water-table that can be watched cheaply and deep pressurized sands that must be pumped from far below, so shallow measurements cannot stand in for deep availability.
findings.scope: Dehgaon locality, Dahegam Taluka, with reference to Unava and Kalol belt

findings.title: Sertha's 353-m layer cake: where water can sit and where it cannot
findings.statement: Sertha's 353-m log starts with topsoil 0-3 m, sand 3-20 m and clay 20-25 m, then alternates brown gravelly sands 5-11 m thick with earthy sticky and variegated clays, including 28-m clay plugs at 175-203 m and 212-240 m, ending in brownish-black clay/claystone with bluish-grey claystone 320-353 m.
findings.why_it_matters: Clean sands are the aquifers people screen; the thick sticky clays are the seals that confine them — their alternation explains why multiple separate pressurized zones exist below 100 m.

findings.title: Kalol's finely logged 200-m stack
findings.statement: Kalol's log to 202.53 m uses centimetre precision and the same sand-silt-clay plus sand-with-gravel/kankar rhythm, with a notably thick 108.28-135.21 m fine sand with gravel and a lower 189.03-202.53 m fine-to-coarse sand at bottom.
findings.why_it_matters: Precise thin layering shows usable sands are not one sheet but several discrete lenses separated by silt and clay — wells must be screened at the right lens, not just drilled deep.

findings.title: Same alluvial motif, three places — plus copy and gap warnings
findings.statement: Palaz and Pethapur repeat the same yellowish sand that coarsens downward versus soapy yellow clay pattern to 202 m with 14-m and 17-m mixed zones at 61-75 m and 177-194 m, while Sardhav extends a browner/redder version of that motif to 344 m but with a 24-m missing section 300-324 m and doubled top sands.
findings.why_it_matters: Repeatability builds confidence that sandy aquifers persist laterally, but the identical Palaz-Pethapur tail and Sardhav's gap/overlap warn that logs need checking before they are used for siting high-yield wells.
findings.scope: Palaz, Pethapur and Sardhav sites, Gandhinagar District

findings.title: What direct well evidence alone cannot prove
findings.statement: The direct logs give only lithology, From-To depth and thickness with site name and taluka; they carry no coordinates, elevation, drilling method or date, logger, water level, screen interval, discharge or quality, and p.104 wells give only Alluvial as aquifer with category ownership and empty remarks.
findings.why_it_matters: Without locations, screens and water levels tied to each sand, you cannot map which sand feeds which village or how much can be pumped safely — the logs must be combined with piezometer levels and pump tests elsewhere in the report.
findings.scope: District litholog and inventory tables pp.99-109

findings.title: Sertha gives the deepest window, bottoming in claystone at 353 m
findings.statement: The Sertha exploratory well is logged continuously from surface to 353 m, the deepest of the five supplied logs, ending in brownish-black clay, claystone and an 18-m mixed sand-clay zone at 325-343 m capped by claystone to 353 m.
findings.why_it_matters: Only Sertha sees below ~250 m, so any claim about deep confined aquifers or basement depth in this part of the district hangs on this one hole; its basal clays act as a marker to hang shallower correlations on.
findings.scope: Sertha EW, Gandhinagar Taluka - deepest district control for fence and cross-section

findings.title: Palaz and Pethapur are near-identical — a caution, not double confirmation
findings.statement: Palaz (0-202 m) and Pethapur (0-202 m) both consist of repeating yellowish sands, soapy slippery clays with 5-10% sand, and mixed zones in 2-18 m beds, and the 61-177 m Pethapur section duplicates the Palaz 61-194 m descriptions verbatim.
findings.why_it_matters: If two logs are copied rather than independently logged, treating them as two separate proofs that a sand layer continues laterally would overstate confidence in aquifer continuity and in taluka-level volume estimates.
findings.scope: Palaz and Pethapur lithologs, district comparison 0-202 m

findings.title: Sardhav adds a 300-m-plus record, but with a gap and overlaps
findings.statement: Sardhav PZ-Gandhinagar is logged from surface to about 300 m with alternating brown coarse-to-medium and fine sands and brown to reddish clays, then resumes at 324-329 m and 329-344 m, leaving a 300-324 m gap and preserving overlapping 0-3 m versus 0-15 m top entries as in the source.
findings.why_it_matters: Sardhav is valuable as a second deep control near Gandhinagar town, but thickness counts for phreatic versus confined zones cannot be taken at face value until the gap is acknowledged and the duplicated top metres are cleaned.
findings.scope: Sardhav PZ-Gandhinagar site, 0-344 m with interruption

findings.title: Not one tank, but stacked sand-and-clay layers
findings.statement: The district works as one shallow unconfined aquifer plus three deeper confined aquifers, visible as alternating sand bodies and clay separators in every complete log.
findings.why_it_matters: A shallow dug well and a deep tube well tap completely different systems; managing them as if they were the same leads to wrong expectations about yield, drying and protection.
findings.scope: Gandhinagar District and Gandhinagar Taluka borehole cluster

findings.title: Khadat shows the shallow sandy window and the deep clay seal
findings.statement: Khadat starts brown and sandy to about 60 m, passes through a 24-m mixed clay at 60-84 m, and then stays in blue-grey clays and sandy clays with only thin sand stringers to 198 m, including sandy clay at 192-198 m.
findings.why_it_matters: It tells drillers and farmers where the easy shallow water ends and where deeper drilling hits seal rather than supply, saving failed bores and pointing to where confinement begins.

findings.title: Neighbouring holes look alike at the top, different below
findings.statement: Chhalla and Chiloda share a sandy top but differ in detail: Chhalla has pinkish-yellow sands, brown to dark-grey gravels at about 13-30 m and grey sands to about 182 m sealed by dark bluish-grey clay at 181.8-200.75 m, while Chiloda has sand with Kankar at 15-30 m and 42-48 m and pink feldspar-quartz sand at 30-42 m before interbedded yellowish-brown clay to 201 m.
findings.why_it_matters: A successful depth in one village cannot be copied blindly next door; local Kankar, gravel and feldspar markers help correlate but also prove lateral change that controls yield and quality.
findings.scope: Chhalla and Chiloda area, Gandhinagar Taluka, 0-201 m

findings.title: Giyod’s deep clays explain the confined aquifers
findings.statement: Giyod proves a thick 64-m quartzite-bearing sand at 52-116 m suitable for supply, separated by very thick sticky grey clays 188-306 m (118 m), 327-406 m (79 m) and 406-450.94 m that act as regional seals.
findings.why_it_matters: Those hundred-metre clays are what keep deep water under pressure and relatively protected; punching through them without care risks connecting systems and losing that natural protection.

findings.title: A superb shallow sand with only a thin cover
findings.statement: Gram Bharti has 40 m of clean, well-sorted sand ideal for shallow wells, a 5-m quartz-feldspar gravel at 40-45 m, and then soapy clay from 45 m downward in a record that stops at 58 m.
findings.why_it_matters: Such clean shallow sands give good water easily but are the first to feel drought, pumping and surface pollution, so they need recharge protection and careful monitoring rather than deep-drilling logic.
findings.scope: Gram Bharti (Amrapur) shallow section 0-58 m, truncated

findings.title: Dahegam has a thick clay seal over shallow basalt, but basement deepens by ~33 m between villages
findings.statement: In Dahegam, Moti Bardoli and Sanmapa both prove a thick clay lid over shallow basalt: Moti Bardoli hits basalt at 235 m after 153 m of greyish-blue sticky clay (82-235 m) and continues in basalt to 293.48 m in four sub-units; Sanmapa hits basalt deeper at 267.9 m after 143.7 m of grey-to-blue sticky hard clay (96.81-240.55 m) and continues to 288.91 m.
findings.why_it_matters: A 140-m-plus clay cap strongly confines deeper water, limiting direct recharge from above but also protecting it from surface pollution; drillers must go 235-268 m to reach hard rock, and deep-well yields depend on basalt fracturing, not alluvial sand.
