findings.title: Giyod proves very thick alluvium with no basement to 451 m and two massive clay blocks
findings.statement: At Giyod-Gandhinagar the borehole goes from topsoil at 0-3 m through fine sands, silts and a 64-m quartzite sand with clay lenses at 52-116 m, then into long clay-dominated sections including 118 m of sticky grey clay at 188-306 m and 79 m of sticky light-grey clay at 327-406 m, reaching ~451 m without encountering basalt or quartzite basement.
findings.why_it_matters: Where clays are 80-120 m thick, they act as regional aquitards that split the system into separate confined aquifers; the 52-116 m quartzite sand is the key heterogeneous aquifer in the upper 150 m, while deeper sands are thin lenses inside clay.

findings.title: Shallow alluvium follows a sand-gravel-clay template that hosts the water-table aquifer
findings.statement: The top 60 m repeats across Gandhinagar logs: Gram Bharti (Amrapur) shows 40 m of well-sorted subrounded sand, then 5 m of quartz-feldspar gravel at 40-45 m, then 13 m of soapy yellowish-brown clay at 45-58 m; Chiloda shows the same idea as topsoil 0-3 m, silty sands 3-15 m, coarse sands with Kankar at 15-30 m and 42-48 m, with pink feldspar and quartz grains at 30-42 m; Khadat and Sertha start identically with 0-3 m topsoil into sand-with-silt.
findings.why_it_matters: Most dug wells and shallow tube wells live in this top 40-60 m; knowing that clean sorted sand gives way to gravel then to first clay tells villagers and planners where to screen wells and where the water table is most vulnerable to drying and contamination.

findings.title: Ranasan shows where the plain ends and fractured basalt begins
findings.statement: Ranasan-Gandhinagar drills through 227.5 m of upper sands, mixed zones and variegated and sticky clays (including 17.9 m variegated clay at 98-116 m and 42.7 m grey-yellow sticky clay at 124.5-167.2 m), then hits basalt at 227.5 m and stays in basalt to 337.56 m through five varieties — fractured, weathered, amygdaloidal with zeolite/calcite and vesicular — with pink-grey rock chips marking the transition.
findings.why_it_matters: Fractured and vesicular basalt can store and transmit water even where there is no sand; identifying the 227-m transition helps explain why deep wells nearby must be designed for hard rock and why water quality can change abruptly at the sediment-basalt contact.

findings.title: Mansa is a deep sediment pile to 452 m with alternating aquifers and thick clay separators
findings.statement: Mansa stays in sediments to great depth: Itadra reaches 452 m with no basalt, alternating brown sand-with-gravel at 31.95-55.76 m, sandy clay with kankar at 55.76-58.62 m, thick reddish-brown sandy clay at 290.6-370.17 m, clean sand at 370.2-376 m and black clay with claystone at 388-394 m; nearby Nardipur Pz reaches 299.31 m as interlayered coarse-gravel sands (notably 169-179 m and 243-248 m) and yellowish/brownish sticky clays, while Charada shows sand-dominated quartz/feldspar sands in its upper 148.8 m.
findings.why_it_matters: No basement means multiple stacked confined sands can be tapped at 100-150 m, 185-210 m and 260-300 m, but the 80-m clay blocks mean wells must be precisely screened and that pumping from one depth may not quickly affect another — crucial for managing declines.

findings.title: A dense well-by-well backbone lets local differences be checked, not assumed
findings.statement: The chapter rests on twelve direct, depth-ordered litholog sequences joining split tables across pages (Chiloda p113-114, Giyod p114, Moti Bardoli-Sanmapa p115-116, Itadra p116-117, Ranasan p117-118, Nardipur p118-119, plus Khadat, Chhalla, Galuden and partial Gram Bharti and Charada), preserving grain size, colour, clay percent, Kankar, gravel and basalt texture at each interval.
findings.why_it_matters: Because every claim can be traced to a named interval and thickness, local planners can see exactly which village log supports an aquifer pick and where more drilling or piezometers are still needed instead of extrapolating from one well to the whole taluka.

findings.title: Mansa Taluka: Four Layers, Deeper Water and Saltier Water With Depth
findings.statement: Mansa is documented as a four-tier system: shallow unconfined sands to about 70 m, then three deeper pressurized sands at about 100-150 m, 185-210 m and 260-300 m, with water levels getting deeper downward and salinity widening downward.
findings.why_it_matters: For a well owner this decides how deep to drill, what pump is needed, and whether deeper really means better. Deeper here often means more lift and a higher chance of brackish water, not automatically safer supply.

findings.title: Kalol Block: Same Cake, Slightly Different Layer Depths
findings.statement: Kalol repeats the same stacked design but with its own depths: a thicker shallow zone to about 90 m and confined tops at about 110, 165 and 240 m, proven by piezometer sands such as pure sand at 53.9-60.8 m and fine sand with gravel at 108-135 m.
findings.why_it_matters: You cannot copy a successful drilling depth from Mansa to Kalol. Even a 10-20 m shift decides whether a well screens a productive sand or a clay, affecting yield and cost.

findings.title: What the Cuttings Show: Thin Sands Sealed by Thick Clays
findings.statement: Foot-by-foot logs show thin productive sands separated by sandy clay and sticky clay, including a massive 82-235 m clay at Moti Bardoli and metre-scale sands like Sertha 3-20 m and Khadat 48-60 m.
findings.why_it_matters: This layering is why two wells 500 m apart can behave differently and why the deep aquifers stay pressurized. The clays are the lids; puncturing or missing them changes water level, quality and vulnerability to over-pumping.

findings.title: Piezometer Proof Up Close: Small Lenses on Top, Better Sands Below
findings.statement: Piezometers at Nardipur, Ranasan and nearby sites prove the near surface is a busy stack of 2-30 m lenses: wind-blown silty topsoil, fine sand, clayey sand, sticky clay and occasional sand-gravel, before thicker medium-to-coarse sands below.
findings.why_it_matters: Shallow inventory and monitoring wells live in those thin top lenses, so they go dry or turn brackish quickly. Deeper piezometers that reach the thicker sands give a truer picture of longer-term storage.

findings.title: Where the Alluvium Ends: Basalt Floor Beneath the Sands
findings.statement: Deep holes bottom out in hard rock: reddish-brown to grey basalt that is vesicular, fractured or weathered in places, and in places quartzite, reddish sandstone and grey claystone just above basalt.
findings.why_it_matters: The basement is a hard stop for groundwater development. Drilling deeper than that floor adds cost without adding alluvial water, and the fractured top of basalt behaves very differently from the sands above.

findings.title: Fresh Next to Brackish: Spot Wells Show Sharp Quality Contrasts
findings.statement: Direct samples only kilometres apart range from fresh at Bhat-II (410 mg/L) and C04 (430 mg/L) to moderately brackish at Kadjodra (1,320 mg/L) and Dingucha-I (1,590 mg/L) to strongly brackish at Nasmed (3,210 mg/L).
findings.why_it_matters: Averages mislead here. Drinking and irrigation planning must be well-by-well: a fresh confined pocket can sit beside an unusable one, and blending or shifting pumpage matters more than district totals.

findings.title: Dahegam's best gravels are sandwiched between clays
findings.statement: At Dahegam the log starts with 0-51 m of sandy soil, yellowish clay, kankar-rich clay and sandy clay, then switches to 51-139 m dominated by gravel, gravel-with-clay and gravel-with-sand in 3-24 m beds, then switches back to clay with gravels 132-139 m and a 61-m-thick clay with 10% kankar from 139-200 m.
findings.why_it_matters: The upper 51 m holds the shallow unconfined water most dug wells tap, the middle gravels are the most promising shallow aquifer, and the thick lower clay is what seals off deeper confined water — so a well screened at 60-80 m behaves very differently from one drilled through the lower clay.

findings.title: Basement rock is shallow in the east, missing at depth elsewhere
findings.statement: Moti Bardoli hit basement at 235 m (grey basalt 235-250 m, soft friable 250-263 m, brown-red 263-281 m, black 281-293.48 m), Ranasan hit it at 227.5 m with zeolite and calcite-filled amygdaloidal basalt to 337.56 m, and Sanmapa hit it at 267.9 m after 21 m of basalt to 288.91 m — while Itadra-Mansa was still in sediments at 452 m and Nardipur was still in sediments at 299.31 m.
findings.why_it_matters: Basement is the bottom of the groundwater system: where it is at 227-268 m you cannot drill deeper for water, where it is absent to 300-450 m there is more room to stack deeper aquifers but also much more clay to drill through.

findings.title: A 140-190 m thick clay wall creates the confined system
findings.statement: Three different deep holes show the same feature: 143-153 m of grey-blue clay at Moti Bardoli and Sanmapa (82-235 m and 96.81-240.55 m) and an even thicker 189.37 m of blue sticky hard clay at 240.33-429.70 m in the 450.43-m-deep continuation hole, underlain by another 20.73 m of blue clay with little sand to 450.43 m.
findings.why_it_matters: This is not a thin parting — it is thicker than a 40-storey building is tall. It is what holds pressure in Confined Aquifers I, II and III below and protects them from surface pollution, but it also means shallow wells and deep wells are tapping completely separate resources.

findings.title: Mansa stays sandy to great depth
findings.statement: Itadra in Mansa stayed in alluvium to 452 m with gravel-with-gravel and kankar markers at 31.95-58.62 m and 266.8-287.73 m and a 79.61-m sandy-clay bed at 290.6-370.17 m, while the nearby Charada upper 0-148.8 m is mostly dull brown and pinkish medium-coarse quartz-feldspar sand with clay breaks under 15 m.
findings.why_it_matters: For Mansa this means the phreatic zone (0-70 m) and Confined Aquifers I (100-150 m) and II (185-210 m) sit inside a much thicker sandy pile than in Dahegam, so there are more sand lenses to target — but also long clay stretches that must be cased off to keep a deep well clean.

findings.title: Water lives in thin, alternating lenses
findings.statement: Kasturinagar-IFFCO (0-44.2 m) alternates topsoil, 9.15 m fine sand, kankar-and-sand, clay, clay-with-silt, sand, kankar-sand-gravel and sand-with-gravel in 3-9 m beds; Sanoda (0-99 m) alternates topsoil, fine sand, silt-clay, sand-with-kankar, sticky reddish-brown clay, mixed sand-clay zones and quartzitic and coarse sands in 3-13 m beds; Nardipur alternates coarse-gravel sands and sticky clays in 12 sub-units with key gravels at 95-121 m (26 m), 169-179 m (10 m) and 243-248 m (5 m).
findings.why_it_matters: A neighbour's successful 30-m well can fail at your plot if you hit a clay lens instead of a sand lens. Well design must match screens to the exact sand or gravel bed logged at that site, not to a district average.

findings.title: What we actually drilled and measured
findings.statement: The synthesis rests on direct well evidence: exploratory holes like Khoraj Dabhi and deep lithologs at Moti Bardoli, Sanmapa, Itadra, Ranasan, Nardipur, Charada, Dahegam, Kasturinagar and Sanoda, tied to a monitoring network that includes Gandhinagar-I and II, Dehgam-I and II, Pundhra, Bhat, Adraj Moti, Kalol and Mansa stations for unconfined, Confined-I and Confined-II water levels and quality.
findings.why_it_matters: It tells a reader how much to trust the taluka stories: they are not modelled guesses but metre-by-metre rock descriptions and repeated water-level and quality measurements at named wells that can be revisited and re-sampled.

findings.title: Kalol piezometer proves stacked sands separated by clays
findings.statement: Kalol Pz starts with topsoil and well-sorted fine sand 0-5.7 m, then silt-clay, yellowish fine-to-coarse sand and sand with kankar and gravel down to 24.07 m, and continues to 202.53 m as alternating sand, clay, silt and mixed zones. Clean aquifer-type sands are logged at 37.57-40.57 m, 44.2-47.2 m, 53.9-60.8 m pure sand, 108.28-135.21 m thick fine sand with gravel, 138.91-145.89 m, 169.01-175.76 m and 189.03-202.53 m fine-to-coarse sand, separated by clay zones such as 27.07-33.82 m, 60.8-67.57 m and 81.27-101.53 m.
findings.why_it_matters: For a non-specialist, think of a layer cake: the sandy layers can hold and give water, the clay layers block it. The log shows several sandy layers, not one continuous supply, so wells must be screened at the right depth and clays can protect deeper water from surface pollution but also limit recharge.
findings.scope: Kalol Taluka - Kalol Pz borehole 0-202.53 m

findings.title: Pore borehole gives a 450-m window into deep sands
findings.statement: Pore-Gandhinagar is the deepest direct record at 450 m. The top is topsoil 0-5 m and fine sand with silt and kankar 5-37 m, then an alternate sand-clay sequence to 172.5 m including coarse sand with gravel at 147-156 m. From 172.5 to 450 m the alternation continues, with yellowish medium-to-coarse sands above and dark brown to dark-coloured medium-to-coarse sands at 320-335 m, 345-354 m and 395-400 m, culminating in two very thick coarse dark sand zones with bluish-grey clay at 354-395 m and 400-450 m.
findings.why_it_matters: Deep, thick sands like the 41-m and 50-m zones at the bottom are the most promising stores for large, sustained supply, but they lie 350-450 m down, so drilling there is costly and water may be older and different in quality. The shallow 32-m sandy cover is where ordinary dug wells tap water first.

findings.title: Clay colour change marks the shift to deep confinement
findings.statement: Above about 248 m the clays are described as yellowish and sticky; from 248-254 m a first bluish-grey patch appears, and from 302-308 m the log records bluish-grey clay with dark sands below. This yellowish to bluish-grey shift separates an upper yellowish sand-clay system from a lower bluish-grey clay plus dark sand system that hosts the thickest deep sands.
findings.why_it_matters: Colour is a practical field clue for drillers and scientists: yellowish usually means oxidised, shallower conditions, while grey-blue often means waterlogged, confined conditions. Recognising the change helps decide where the unconfined top ends and where deeper, more protected confined aquifers begin.

findings.title: Sanoda shallow log shows why every few metres matter
findings.statement: Sanoda-Gandhinagar 3-99 m shows fine light-brown sand, light-yellow silt-clay, sand with kankar, reddish-brown sticky clay, and mixed sand-clay zones, with notable sands at 44-51 m quartzitic sand with clay lenses, 55-68 m fine sand with silt, 68-78 m mixed sand-clay, 78-85 m coarse sand with kankars and 88-99 m coarse sand with gravel. A further 99.0-200.5 m tail of 101.5 m is preserved as interbedded sticky grey and light-brown clay with fine-to-coarse light-brown sand, mixed sand-clay, sand-kankar-clay lenses and sand-silt-clay zones.
findings.why_it_matters: Even in the first 100 m, water-bearing sands come in thin 4-13 m slices separated by clay. A well that stops a few metres too shallow or screens across clay may yield little water or muddy water, so this metre-by-metre record guides correct well depth and screen placement for villages.

findings.title: What the wells do not yet prove
findings.statement: Pages 122-124 join cleanly at 172.5 m for Pore and at 24.07 m for Kalol, confirming two continuous boreholes, but page 125 yielded no extractable text, tables or figures despite drawing flags, and the 99-200.5 m tail rows carry no locality name in the extraction. Decimal points were also lost in the raw tables so 1725 means 172.5 m and 2407 means 24.07 m, as confirmed by thickness checks.
findings.why_it_matters: Blank or unresolved pages are not absence of geology - they are absence of usable evidence in this extraction. Decisions should not assume basement depth or taluka-wide continuity from these logs alone; the original drawings and missing locality for the tail need to be checked before using them for new well siting.

uncertainties.statement: Detailed GEC-15 inputs like rainfall, specific yield zones and draft calculation factors for pages 46-47 were not in the extract, only totals, so taluka recharge differences cannot be fully explained.
Map Figure 20 categorisation and Figure 26 feasible-area geometry were caption-only with no coordinates or legend values, so spatial boundaries cannot be verified.
Feasible recharge area total 2224.73 sq km exceeds Table-25 district area 2163.00 sq km, indicating an area-base inconsistency to reconcile before local planning.

Table 21 suitability lists only Dahegam Soft Rock with percolation tanks, recharge wells and shafts; rows for Gandhinagar, Kalol and Mansa were blank in extraction and should be treated as missing, not as unsuitable.
Ledger scaling artifacts noted in source tables (for example water-required totals shown larger by factors of 10-1000) require careful unit checking before use in budgets.

Projection to ~97.29% district stage assumes phased MIS adoption (~15% of balance area per year) and the stated draft formula; actual savings depend on crop delta, adoption rate and sharing of partnership wells.
Supplied evidence references feasible recharge areas and the 200-300 m Group-III deep aquifer occurrence but does not quantify deep-zone storage, quality or safe yield in this partition.
Taluka draft-after-MIS and stage-after values are source projections, not monitored outcomes; Mansa remaining above 120% indicates residual risk even if targets are met.
TDS units not printed in annexure tables; conventionally assumed mg/L.
Ledger decimals for pH, fluoride, iron, potassium and conductance needed correction against page image (e.g., 810 to 8.10).
Coordinates given to 2-8 decimals with several truncated to 2 decimals and no CRS/datum stated, limiting precise mapping.
Unava latitude 24.3675 is far north of cluster 23.07-23.48 and needs verification as possible typo.
Confined table gives no depth, screen, well-type or lab method, so co-located differences cannot be tied to a specific layer.
Unconfined TDS range 350-1320 and confined range 400-3210 are May-2017 snapshots only; seasonal and yearly change not shown.
No drinking-water standard values are given in the supplied evidence slice, so formal potable versus non-potable classification cannot be made here.
Results represent a single month (May 2017) for the shallow aquifer only; seasonal change and deep confined-aquifer quality are not covered by the supplied rows.
Source rows are flagged needs_review and include split village names and coordinate parsing, so small transcription uncertainty remains.
Figures of sections, fence diagram and 3-D model were listed but geometry values were not text-extractable; descriptions rely on captions and legends.
Aquifer-F and Aquifer-G share identical depth and thickness values in the source table, suggesting a duplication that cannot be resolved as separate geometries.
Feasibility table pairings of well depth to discharge (10–25 m with 200–300 lpm versus 50–100 m with 600–800 lpm) are ambiguous in extraction and treated as typical ranges, not well-specific tests.
Eastern correlation is noted as difficult where alluvium is thin and clay partings are thin; aquifer identities there are less certain than in the well-developed western succession.
No borehole-wise picks, thicknesses or coordinates were given in the extracted text; cross-section and fence/3D geometry is qualitative and numeric depths are not reliably readable from figures.
Depth ranges for successive aquifers overlap (e.g., 35-90 m vs 55-150 m), reflecting lateral variation and interpretation rather than strict horizontal boundaries.
Place-name spelling variants (Pilvai/Pilwai, Sardhav/Sarthav, Gamij/Ghamij, Khoraj Dhabi/Dabhi) and transect endpoint wording were preserved without coordinates.
Table 12 prints TDS units as Mg/l [sic] interpreted as mg/l; transmissivity for the unconfined aquifer is reported as '-' (not reported).
Population cited as 1,391,753 in the at-a-glance table versus 1,387,478 in the descriptive text; both refer to 2011 Census and 252 villages.

Average rainfall cited as 744 mm in the summary table, ~739 mm normal for 1930-60, and 799.6 mm total in the Ahmedabad proxy climatology table; differences reflect period, station and rounding, not error in trend.

Crop-area table is OCR-garbled with implausible values (e.g., castor, guar, fennel) and overlapping land-use categories whose tabulated sq km sum exceeds district area; use crop names qualitatively, not exact areas.
Climate, temperature, humidity and wind are from Ahmedabad Airport outside the district with unspecified coordinate system; they are representative, not measured inside Gandhinagar.
Elevation range 56-126 m amsl and lat-long to minute precision lack stated datum/CRS, and Table-1 headers are split across rows; treat as district-level reference for maps, not for site survey.
Geographic area is cited as 216,300 ha in narrative but 215,838 ha in the taluka table (462 ha gap); Kalol net sown repeats Gandhinagar's 48,767 ha, suggesting a copying error.
Climate is proxied by Ahmedabad IMD station with no in-district station; monthly table totals 799.6 mm versus 739 mm normal quoted in text — different periods or sources unclear.
Summer 2017-18 taluka areas sum to 30,881 ha versus stated district total 22,912 ha — arithmetic inconsistency; table header also mislabels summer as 'Ravi season'.

Kharif, rabi and summer tables are single-year (2017-18) snapshots from Season and Crop Reports with no methods, dates or coordinates; 10-year and 3-year averages shown only for rabi and summer totals.
Population, household and settlement pattern were not included in the supplied evidence for this partition.
Soil types, fertility and soil-water properties were not included in the supplied evidence.
Precise district location, boundaries and neighbouring districts were not stated in the supplied evidence.
Season-wise cropped area and irrigation source split (canal vs groundwater vs other) could not be reliably quantified because Mansa summer and district summer totals are flagged inconsistent.
Topographic elevations, slope and detailed drainage network beyond the three named rivers were not provided.
Table 18 Sr.No 7, 12, 13, 14 are absent in the source, so the Confined Group-II station list is incomplete.
One Confined Group-I row labels Amrapur Pzii value +1.072162 as Fall despite positive sign; direction was preserved as in source.
Phreatic zonal ranges 10-50 and 50-70 mbgl are reported identical for May and November 2017 despite different extrema, suggesting rounded map interpretation rather than precise re-measurement.
Several unconfined trend values have garbled extraction (for example Hilol 15343 Rise, Rakhiyal 11450 Rise) and duplicate Devkaran Na Muvada rows with different trends were kept as distinct records.

Units and formulae are not explicitly labelled in headers; metres below ground level for depths and fluctuation as decadal average minus 2017 are inferred from arithmetic consistency (e.g., 38.46-33.3=5.16; 82-33.3=48.7).
Many early October cells are blank (e.g., Sr.3-8 only 2012-2016 present; Sr.21 missing 2007-2010 and 2016), so decadal averages cover different periods and are not strictly comparable.
Extraction fragments split village, taluk and numeric tokens across rows (e.g., Bhat-II, Valad, Adalaj Pz-III); values were reassembled from page text and need review against original PDF.
Adalaj Pz-III is listed under the Unconfined annexure with ALV geology despite piezometer naming that suggests confined monitoring; aquifer assignment for Sr.21 should be treated cautiously.
Groundwater flow direction for November 2017 is listed as an observation type but no direction or gradient values were supplied in the evidence, so flow interpretation is not included.

Theme mentions local rises near rivers and canals and over-development, but no river/canal proximity or draft data were supplied; the Kalol rise and Sanoda recovery cannot be attributed to a specific cause from this evidence alone.
Year and pre/post-monsoon assignment for upper-table stations 23-27 cannot be established from garbled headers; values preserved as series only.
Unava Confined-I latitude 24.3675 is an outlier versus ~23.1-23.48 for all other stations and may be a data entry error.
Blank continuation rows containing only ALV token are not distinct stations and were excluded.

Groundwater flow direction and post-monsoon depth recovery, village decadal rises near rivers/canals, and 2008-2017 trend slopes are named in the theme but no usable values were supplied in this extract.
Table extraction is fragmented with split numbers and missing early years for Dingucha-II, Bhoyan Moti and others, so exact yearly values carry uncertainty.
The abrupt Pethapur rise from about 78.5 m to about 106.5 m between 2013 and 2014 needs source verification before use in regulation.
Pre-monsoon May 2017 and post-monsoon November 2017 depths and east-west flow values were not fully preserved in the supplied rows, so seasonal change magnitudes remain indicative.
Paired sites share coordinates but differ in depth and aquifer tag, and name variants like Dehgam versus Dahegam add matching uncertainty.
